text: The market for Government obligations is entering a new phase after being under the pressure of Federal Reserve System anti-inflation sales for the last six months. The changed atmosphere, although not yet clearly definable, is suggestive of. a market steadiness— that is, price stability as distinct from price inflexibility—for both the longest-term and shortest-term Treasury obligations for the foreseeable future.</br></br>The market’s new mood, visible since last Tuesday, is linked by the financial district to the implications of the Korean war, along with possible other factors. For the moment, anyway, there has been a cessation of central bank sales of the Treasury’s longest-term bonds at declining prices.</br></br>More distinctly discernible is a concurrent stabilization in the short-term part of the market. The pattern of bids now underlying all Treasury obligations maturing in fourteen months or less seems to indicate the maintenance indefinitely of the current 1^4 per cent borrowing rata for the Treasury's shortest-term interest-bearing oo-ligations. The new issue of 1% per cent notes which will mature on Aug. 1, 1951, was quoted all week on the premium yield basis of 1.24 per cent bid, 1.22 per cent asked.</br></br>The statistical net result of Federal Reserve operations in the market from June 21 to June 28 was a commentary in itself. During this week, which covered the subscription period to the Treasury’s new 1% per cent note issue, the central banking system’s holdings of Government obligations increased $538,500,000, the largest weekly increase since Septemher of last year. Holdings of bonds were reduced by only $6,000,000, the smallest weekly reduction since January.</br></br>felt, as before, by the Victory 2%s, callable in 1967. Other non-bank bonds were bid up progressively and closed the week at their best prices. On the other hand, bonds eligible for bank investment seemed unsure of their market status from here on in, especially the partly tax-exempt issues, whose market status is affected peculiarly by the proposed reconstitution of the corporate income tax on a 21 per cent normal, 20 per cent surtax basis. It would be imprudent, however, to view the market’s ‘‘new look” as anything more than a espot phenomenon marking a respite from a protracted period of central bank restraint whose tenure and extent have kept the investment .world, guessing for months. In fact, the financial implications of any new “defense effort" are, if anything, only a threat of more inflation—the very Federal Reserve sanction for “selling the market down.”

text: Installment lending by Federal Reserve member banks of this district now amounts to two-fifths of such credit in the country as a whole, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported yesterday.</br></br>Commercial banks, it pointed out, have steadily penetrated the field since the early 1930’s to become the largest source of such loans. _</br></br>In the current issue of its Monthly Review, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York pointed out that in this district member bank installment loans to individuals have increased approximately 760 per cent, from the war-depressed low of $95,000,000 in June, 1944, to $813,000,000 at the end of last year. The growth of such loans in these banks, it was noted, has been paralleled by that in member banks in the country as a whole.</br></br>At the end of 1949, it was pointed out, the largest single component of consumer installment loans was $235,000,000 of retail installment paper other than for automobiles. And this, the bank observed, contrasts with the situation in the remainder of the country, where the largest segment of member banks' installment loans consists of automobile paper. Personal installment cash loans, at $219,000,000, were the next largest component in this district, while repair and modernization loans amounted to $186,000,000, and automobile loans had the smallest total, $162,000,000.</br></br>“The greatest percentage increase during the 1946-49 period, however, occurred in automobile paper,” the bank commented. “This increase was bolstered by the especially large gains in the holdings of a few New York City banks, which have charged relatively low rates on personal loans.

text: PRINCETON, N. J., Dec. 14—A program to curb inflation in the wake of expanding defense expenditures was recommended today by 220 economists representing twenty-seven of the nation’s colleges and universities.</br></br>Designed to constitute “the first line of defense against inflation,” the program calls for elimination of all unnecessary Government expenditures, raising tax revenues faster than defense spending grows to create a cash surplus, find more stringent credit restrictions.</br></br>The statement, drafted by a group of Princeton University economists, was circulated for signatures and released today by Prof. Richard A. Lester of Princeton.</br></br>The signers include Joseph S. Davis of Stanford and I. Leo Sharfman of Michigan; • both former presidents of the American Economic Association; Seymour E. Harris of Harvard, Edward S. Mason, dean of the Graduate School of Public Administration at Harvard; Arthur R. Upgre?n of Minnesota, Ray B. Westerfield of Yale and Clair Wilcox of Swarthmore.</br></br>The undersigned economists believe that prevention of inflation in the situation created by the expanding defense program requires as the principal line of defense, a substantial increase in taxation, reductions in expenditures at all governmental levels wherever this can be done without impairing national defense or other essential public services, and a more restrictive credit policy. The ba-sio cause of inflation, an excess of money demand relative to available goods, must be attacked. Only adequate fiscal and monetary measures can remove this basic cause.

text: The sources of inflation are too numerous and varied to permit a single or "painless" process of correction, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York declares in its annual report, issued today. The problem is not insoluble, however, the bank observes, adding that the challenge to public policy is to find and accept those techniques of control which will be effective during a period of rearmament that may last for years.</br></br>Signed by Allan Sproul, president, the report points out that 1950 presented a paradoxical record of economic change. The national economy, up to the middle of the year, had given a striking demonstration of the recuperative power and capacity for growth ‘‘of an enterprise system largely free of detailed Government intrusion.”</br></br>But by the end of the year, the report continues, the United States found itself—partly because of its success in maintaining a high-consumption economy at virtual full employment—"applying strict controls in order to make room for what was as yet a very moderate expansion in military production.” "Some of those who were strongly urging imposition of direct controls during the last half of 1950 did not recognize the essential interdependence between such measures and general fiscal and credit controls,” the report • observes.</br></br>“This was wishful thinking. Although there was no need of despair of bringing the inflation under control, its sources were too many and too varied to permit reliance upon a single corrective, or to expect the process of correction to be wholly painless.” Limitations on immediate expansion of production last year were the characteristic bottlenecks of full employment, principally a shortage of manpower in the labor force, and. a scarcity of certain critical materials,</br></br>"And the extensive rearrangement of productive capacity and manpower inevitable in the present transition period may be expected temporarily to interfere with the needed growth in productivity,” the report continues.

text: WASHINGTON, July 10—The Federal Reserve Board declined today to relax its restrictions on credits to consumers for installment buying. Its policies in this respect have been under considerable attack in Congress.</br></br>In identical letters to Senator Burnet R. Maybank, Democrat of South Carolina, and Representative Brent Spence, Democrat of Kentucky, chairmen, respectively, of the Banking Committees of the Senate and of the House of Representatives, William McC. Martin Jr., chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, made clear his agency’s position against adding further inflationary pressures to the credit structure of the nation this time.</br></br>The rstrictions on consumer credit, as embodied in the board's Regulation W, “have been effective and salutary in helping to counteract inflationary forces,” Mr. Martin wrote to the two monetary committee chairmen. The curbs in Regulation W, Mr. Martin continued, have operated in conjunction with the more important influences the board has exercised in the field of reserve requirements $or Federal Reserve Banks, open-market operations in support of government bonds, and alterations in the discount rates for commercial .paper.</br></br>The system’s board has taken note, he declared, of the pressures exerted on the two committees by spokesmen for manufacturers and business men who sincerely believe their inventories have become oppressively large because the public is discouraged from buying by the relatively high down-payments and short periods for installments as prescribed by the board.</br></br>As a result, both committees have recommended inclusion in the new Defense Production Act, now under debate in the House, after the emergence from the Senate of a version unsatisfactory to the Administration, statutory requirements that down payments of not more than one-third, and instalments to run at least eighteen months, should be prescribed by law.

text: WASHINGTON, June 7—President Truman declared today that extension and strengthening of the Defense Production Act was needed to prevent ‘‘an unmanageable torrent of inflation.”</br></br>He said existing controls have "stopped the upward rush of prices,” but warned that it was ‘‘only a breathing spell” before defense expenditures, increasing at the rate of $30,000,000,000 during the next year, enlarge terrific inflationary pressures.</br></br>The American people, the President said, are wondering whether existing controls, which expire June 30, will be extended on- a strengthened basis to meet this growing danger. text: Relaxation of restrictive monetary policies by the Federal Reserve in the late spring now appears to have constituted the most important single development in the improved earnings position of large New York City banks.</br></br>Due to a “time lag,” only partial indication of the current bank prosperity will be provided by the third-quarter condition statements and interim earning reports to be published this week, but the outlines of the general improvement are I rapidly emerging.</br></br>Such benefits as the higher level of interest rates on loans and securities, stabilization of deposit totals and the midyear reduction of reserve requirements have yet to make their full impact on operating results. Moreover, with the expiration of the Excess Profits Tax Law in prospect, barring a prolonged recession, the earnings outlook was never more favorable.</br></br>According to M. A. Schapiro & Co., Inc., bank analysts, this year’s net operating earnings of tile seventeen large metropolitan banks after taxes, but before security transactions and transfers to reserves, are likely to be in excess of $170,000,000, a gain of 6.8 per cent over 1952. Such a total would represent a net return of 7 per cent on the banks’ aggregate capital funds of $2,500,000,000. Based on existing rates, dividend payments of $98,000,000, would mean a “payout” of 57 per cent against 60 per cent in 1952.</br></br>In the late spring the Federal Reserve Board acted to provide reserves to the banks by open market purchases of Treasury bills, and by cutting legal reserve requirements against deposits. The cut released $1,156,000,000 of otherwise immobilized assets, and in New York where the requirement was 24 per cent, the 2 per cent reduction made $400,000,000 avail-ble. Combined, these moves were intended to create a primary market for government securities, enabling the banks to participate in the Treasury’s essential financing of about $6,000,000,000 of tax anticipation certificates. The rate for this nine-month money was 2 \'2 [per cent, and because of the avail-lability of the funds provided them, the banks were converted from involuntary sellers, to ready, willing j and able buy ess.

text: For the first time in two decades, the stock market is undergoing a detailed Federal study. The last inquiry, conducted in the gloomiest days of the depression, resulted in stringent laios to regulate security transactions. Now, with, stock prices at record levels, the Senate Banking Committee is trying to determine whether new Government action is called for. Here is ait A-B-C explanation, in the form of questions and answers, of some of the tilings the committee is looking into.</br></br>A.—Stocks represent shares of ownership In a specific enterprise. Some companies have only a few shares of stock; ot.hers have millions. General Motors, the country’s biggest manufacturing corporation, has 92,894,500 shares of common stock and 2,835,644 shares of preferred stock. The owners of a company's stock are the owners of the company. They are entitled to vote for its directors and in that way to exercise a voice, proportionate to their ownership, in the control of its affairs.</br></br>Shares earn money for their owners in the form of dividends. These represent the amount voted to stockholders by the company’s directors on the basis of its income, financial needs and prospects. In most cases preferred stock calls for a fixed dividend, usually at the rate of 4 or 5 per cent of the face value of the stock each year, and the holders of these securities must get their dividends before owners of common stock get anything.</br></br>dividend at all. How much profit a company makes is the primary factor in determining how much it will distribute in dividends. Most companies try, however, to maintain a steady rate of dividends. In good years, extra dividends may be declared. In bad years, dividends may be cut or eliminated.</br></br>A.—Generally, when people speak of the stock market, they think in terms of trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Eighty-five per cent, in dollar value, of all securities bought or sold in organized exchanges are traded on its floor. Listed on the "Big Board" are the shares of 1,200 companies, with more than 10,000,000 employes. These companies produce 90 per cent of the nation’s steel and oil, handle 95 per cent of its rail and air travel, make 70 per cent of its automobiles and trucks, and generate 75 per cent of its privately produced power. The market value of their stock is $170,000,000,000 at current prices. In addition to the New York Stock Exchange, there are a score of smaller market places for the transfer of stock. The largest of these is the American Stock Exchange, formerly the Curb Exchange, in this city. Many stocks are not listed on any exchange. They are traded directly in what are known as “over-the-counter" sales.

text: The last Wall Street investigation prior to the recent “friendly-study” of the-stock market by Senator Fulbright’s Committee on Banking and Currency was not, as many persons believe, the Pecora inquiry of 1933-34. It was the so-called anti-monopoly investigation conducted by the Temporary National Economic Committee half a decade after I that.</br></br>i Far and away the biggest offensive mounted by the committee on that occasion was an I elaborate effort to show that a I handful of banking firms in New York’s financial district had for years held a tight monopolistic grip on the nation’s security underwriting business.</br></br>That inquiry—sometimes referred to,' with the Pujo hearings of 1912 in mind, as the Second Money Trust Investigation— was destined to have a strangely unhappy epilogue a decade and a half later. It was revived on Oct. 30, 1947, in the form of an anti-trust suit in the New York District Court. Judge Harold R. Medina listened for more than two and a half years to the presentation of the Government’s case, then threw it out of court without even calling upon the defendants for a rebuttal.</br></br>Many will recall that inquiry, however, for a less epic and more beguiling distinction. They will remember it as the only Congressional inquiry in which the authors employed, the professional services of an expert in semantics. This tutor, selected, presumably, because he had just produced a popular work on that subject, provided for the committee’s guidance a short vocabulary in which words and phrases were evaluated not for preciseness of meaning, but in terms of their emotional content.</br></br>Many will recall, no doubt, the author’s observations, for example, on possible references to "Government spending.” "Spending," he warned >the committee, “is a ‘bad’ word. Avoid it like a copperhead!” If a situation should arise in which its employment was unavoidable, then, he counseled, it should be “firmly associated with ’sales,’ ’wages,’ ‘purchasing power,’ or other ‘good’ words, tenderly regarded on the folkways.’’ study of the stock market might make history by turning out pretty much as its author intended it should when he first proposed it, back in January. The hearings were certainly not unduly inquisitorial (some may wonder, indeed, whether they were inquisitorial enough). If they strayed into fields that at times seemed only very tenously related to the question at hand this was ascribable, by and large, not to. any tendency on the part of the committee, or its chairman to transform the hearings into a fishing expedition, but to the witnesses themselves. Some of the latter, at least, while by no means reluctant to give the committee the full benefit of their opinions, appeared to find £he subject that they had'come to Washington to discuss either too specific or too confining for their talents.

text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 28-Mention “resort to the printing press” and the man who abhors inflation (and who doesn’t?) shudders. But, at the moment, the notably anti-inflationary United States Treasury is asking Congress for renewal of the Government’s only direct authority to do just that.</br></br>Yet, even though this is the sort of thing that watered such foreign currencies as the French franc, there appears little reason for loss of sleep among the brotherhood of anti-inflationists. The Treasury has no intention of using .the authority except for very brief periods and for largely technical reasons.</br></br>The authority in question is what one student has called the “quicksand of currencies”—the right of a government to borrow directly from the central bank. In this case, it is the right of the Treasury to borrow from the Federal Reserve System.</br></br>Where does the Federal Reserve get the money ? It creates the money, right out of thin air. It doesn’t actually use a printing press, but it creates checking money, which is the same thing.</br></br>at the twelve Federal Reserve Banks are arbitrarily increased by the amount of the borrowing, and the Federal Reserve Banks get what amount to promissory notes in return. There is suddenly more money available for use in the country than there was before, with no more goods to spend it on. That is the very essence of inflation.

text: WASHINGTON, Nov. 17 — Probably the single most important domestic goal of the Eisenhower Administration is to prove that a modem economy can have full employment over an extended period without inflation.</br></br>The evidence of the Administration’s first four years is not conclusive. text: WASHINGTON, May 2—The staff of the Federal Reserve Board concluded in a study made public today that “there is real question” whether there can "soon” be another surge of automobile buying on credit like that of 1955. The conclusion was reached in the final volume of the board’s massive six-volume study of consumer credit. The other five were made public several weeks ago. Today’s volume comprised a survey of the automobile market and financing practices in 1954 and 1955. The key conclusion was: “For the automobile market in 1955, credit factors were plainly of great importance in determining the volume of buyer demand. With credit commitments of new car buyers averaging one-third of their annua! incomes, with the interval between purchases of new cars on credit reduced, with low down payments and long maturities typical, and with many buyers reporting themselves reluctant to incur again long-period car-purchase debt, there is real question whether credit purchases of the 1955 magnitude can be repeated soon.” 9By the second half of 1955 two-thirds of all credit purchases of cars had terms of thirty months or longer, and thirty-six-month terms were "quite common.” Almost half of the credit purchases had l"real" down payments of less |than 25 per cent of, the “real”</br></br>Pin general, low down payments and extra-long maturities went together. Both were associated with lower-income groups.</br></br>Q However, an outstanding development in 1955 was the large growth in the numbers of people in the middle and upper income ranges who bought autos on credit.</br></br><3The average monthly payment was the same in both 1954 and 1955—$72. Car prices were higher in 1955, but credit maturities were extended. Because incomes were a little higher in 1955, the "burden" of the monthly payment declined slightly. The “median” payment amounted to 15 per cent of monthly disposable income — meaning half of the buyers ijaid more and half less.</br></br>1 Almost two out of five of those credit buyers with aftertax incomes of $5,000 or less paid one-fourth or more of their monthly income for automobile payments.

text: WASHINGTON, June 28 — Representative Wilbur D. Mills today challenged "any one” to dispute the conclusion that the Government at present "must rely on general fiscal and monetary restraints to curb inflation.”</br></br>The Arkansas Democrat emphasized, in an unusual letter sent to every member of Congress, that a recent report of a joint subcommittee that he headed did not “endorse” tight money or high taxes. He said all members of the group “want to see substantial reductions in taxes and easing of monetary restraints.” “But no member of the subcommittee on fiscal policy, no member of the Joint Economic Committee, no ipember of the Congress wants further inflation.”</br></br>A Democratic Storm The Mills letter' clearly resulted from, the storm caused in Democratic circles by the unanimous report Wednesday of his Joint Economic subcommittee. The report, which backed monetary restraint and opposed tax cuts in the present state of the economy,, cut across a Democratic challenge to the tight money policy.</br></br>“There is only one way in which taxes can be reduced and monetary restraints eased without resulting in further inflation, so long as the economy continues to operate at high .and rising levels. That one way is by stopping the increases in Federal Government spending.” Actually, a number of Democrats in Congress have argued that tight money is the wrong policy to fight this particular inflation, which they say is not a "classic” inflation of excessive demand and spending. Mr. Mills said that he regretted “very much” that “the report has not been received in all quarters in the nonpartisan spirit in which it was offered.”</br></br>“The basic problem undertying present inflationary trends is an inadequate level of real savings out of current income. Until higher levels of voluntary real savings are achieved, we must rely on general fiscal and] monetary restraints to curb inflation. The burdens of high, taxes and tight money do not fall evenly throughout the economy. But the burden of infla,-tion is far more unevenly distributed."

text: In an editorial dealing with the stock market decline, appearing in this newspaper on Oct. 10, it was observed that “such a readjustment, however painful, was overdue.” The editorial went on to add: “It is not a healthy sign for the economy when corporate stock prices reach the point where they yield less to the holder than he can obtain from corporate bonds."</br></br>Two days after that The Times published a letter to the editor from a correspondent who "wondered” whether it wouldn’t be possible to improve the paper’s “timing” of such comments. “Couldn’t the Times,” the writer inquired, “deal with such aberrations at an earlier stage” ?</br></br>The short and obvious answer to this, of course, would be that The Times, in common with most responsible newspapers, probably didn’t regard it as part of its editorial function to pro-vide its readers with a stock market tipster service. Few editors in full possession of their senses, it is fair to say, would knowingly indulge in what the onetime chief editorial writer for The Wall Street Journal, William Peter Hamilton, once referred to as “the most gratui-! tous form of human folly” —namely, attempting to call the turn on the stock market.</br></br>A few days ago A. Wilfred May of The Commercial and Financial Chronicle, in an address delivered before a price forecasting seminar of the Econometric Institute, took the occasion to recall a classic observation on this subject by the late Lord Keynes. Said Keynes: “Professional investment may be likened to those newspaper competitions in which the competitors have to pick out the six prettiest faces from 100 photographs; the prize being awarded to the competitor whose choice most nearly corresponds to the average preferences of the competitors as a whole. Each competitor has to pick,</br></br>not those faces which he himself finds prettiest but those which he thinks are likely to catch the fancy of the other competitors, all of whom are looking at the problem from the same point of view.” Not even the Federal Reserve Board, which has the power to restrain speculative activity through the raising and lowering of mandatory mimimum margins, would think of intervening in the market on the basis of its own arbitrary decision that stocks were priced too high. It had not exercised these powers in the more than two years between its last margin rise, in April, 1955, and the recent downturn in stock prices. It has refrained from doing so, and quite correctly, despite the fact that stock prices advanced roughly 80 points, as measured by The Times average, since the first of its two most recent margin increases, in January, 1955.

text: SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 9— On the eve of his eighty-third birthday anniversary, Herbert Hoover sighted two clouds over the country today. One was “the cloud of inflation,” the other, the “possibility of war.”</br></br>The thirty-first President of the United States said he had one predominant hope for the world: “Peace.”</br></br>Mr. Hoover termed the inflation situation “very dangerous.” He said the purchasing power of the dollar had dropped five or six cents during “the last recurrent period” of an inflationary trend; but he viewed the policies of "the Eisenhower Administration, the Federal Reserve Banks and collateral financial agencies” as “unquestionably bringing the thing to check.”</br></br>Mr. Hoover voiced the conviction that the free world had “grown distinctly stronger” since his eighty-second anniversary. He said he was not comparing it and the Communist countries wholly on the basis of military strength, but on “general balance.” “I don’t know anybody who can evaluate nuclear arms,” he said. “We can evaluate armies and navies but nobody can evaluate relative nuclear strength, especially when we know nothing about our major enemy — Russia.”</br></br>“I have not the gift of prophecy, like Isaiah. I don’t know. I can make no useful comment. You listen to Mr. [Nikita S.] Khrushchev [First Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party] one day, and the next day to somebody else.” ON BIRTHDAY EVE: Former President Herbert Hoover posing yesterday .atop the Mark Hopkins Hotel in San Francisco. Mr. Hoover will celebrate eighty-third birthday today. In background are Telegraph Hill and Coit Tower.

text: PRICES, wholesale and retail, up about 6 per cent in the last two years, have shown signs of leveling off recently.</br></br>| This may seem a far-fetched, if not^ downright weird warning in the light of the present business slump. Yet facts are facts, and this is what they shov?:</br></br>There has been no general decline in prices despite the broad drops in production and in other major segments of the economy. Industrial production late last summer was running at 145 per cent of the 1947-49 average; by December it had fallen to 136 per cent and there was undoubtedly another dip in January. Over the same period —when the economy was obviously moving into a recession stage—wholesale and consumer prices continued to rise. The indexes did remain stationary in December and possibly in January. text: A year ago this month the Government released statistics confirming what many had suspected •—that the 1957-58 recession was the worst since World War II. One showed that in April 1958, 5.1 million were unemployed—7.5 per cent of the labor force, a post-war record. Another showed that industrial production for the month was at a recession low of 126 per cent of the 1947-49 average (compared with a pre-recession high of 146 in February, 1957).</br></br>Last week, the Government released the unemployment and industrial production reports for April, 1959. These are the statistics for each: 735,000 to 3.6 million, the lowest since December, 1957. Employment rose by 1.8 million to 65 million, an April record. (The all-time high was 67.2 million in July, 1957.) The rate of unemployment dropped to</br></br>5.3 per cent, compared with 5.8 f>er cent in March, and was about two-thirds of the way back to the prerecession level of 4 to 4.5 per cent. A Labor Department spokesman noted that despite improvement there was “still a problem’’—longterm unemployment. The number of men out of work more than fifteen weeks was 1.4 million. This was 150,000 fewer than last month, but twice as many as two years ago. They account for 38.5 per cent of all unemployment.</br></br>1957.” Consumer incomes and buying “were at record levels” and “housing starts remained at exceptionally high level.”</br></br>It is now more than eight months since Gov. Orval E. Faubus of Arkansas closed the four Little Rock high schools rather than obey Supreme Court orders to resume an integration program. Of the 3,665 students involved, 2,646 are attending classes, most of them in private schools at Little Rock, the rest in public schools elsewhere; 440 are taking correspondence courses; and 579 are doing neither. The four schools stand idle. This situation has led to increasing restiveness in Little Rock. Last December this was aggravated by the election of a six-man school board (the old one resigned) which found itself in deadlock—three pro-Faubus segregationists versus three moderates who favor reopening the schools with “controlled” integration.

text: Poverty in the midst of plenty. This may seem an inappropriate phrase to apply to the New York money market banks, those dozen or so multi-billion dollar institutions whose combined assets are almost one-fifth the resources of all Federal Reserve member banks in the United States.</br></br>Nevertheless, tile phrase is descriptive of a situation that has prevailed since the nation's money managers began to shift early this year from a policy of credit restraint to one of ease. For although the Federal Reserve has pumped well above $2,000,000,000 in new reserves into the banking system, the New York banks find themselves forced to live pretty much from hand to mouth as far as reserves are concerned.</br></br>In the next two weeks, the money managers will make their largest single addition so far in the present period of ease to the supply of these “high-powered dollars,” dollars that the banks can use to support additional loans and investments in the ratio roughly of $7 of new loans and investments for each new dollar of reserves.</br></br>On Thursday, the 6,200 Federal Reserve member banks will be permitted to count all the cash in their vaults and tills as reserves, something they have been permitted to do only partially until now. This is expected to provide $150,000,000 in new reserves for banks in New York and Chicago, $380,000,000 for banks in other large cities, and $900,000,000 for so-called country banks, those in smaller cities and towns.</br></br>For the country banks, the gain will be offset to the extent of $380,000,000 by an increase from 11 to 12 per cent ini the percentage of deposits re-j iquired to be immobilized in cash with the Federal Reserve i Banks, making the net increase I for them $520,000,000.

text: President Kennedy was asked at his news conference last week whether he had purposely avoided using the word “recession” in a speech the previous day about the national economy. He replied that “to put it precisely * * * I would call this a recession."</br></br>At the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue, Senate Republican Leader Everett Dirksen said "recede means to come down from a high level, and in that respect I guess we have a recession.” He went on to say, however, that statements such as the President’s may "talk the country into a recession.”</br></br>This semantic contest underscored the sharp contrast in attitude between the White House and the Capitol over the state of the economy. President Kennedy took office convinced that the nation was in a slump, and he.set out immediately to apply restoratives. He has ordered a variety of stimulants on his own authority and has bombarded Congress with requests for the kind that require legislation.</br></br>But so far Congress has adopted none of the President’s proposals and in most cases has not even begun action on them. This attitude stems partly from Congress’ traditional lethargy in its opening weeks. But a more fundamental problem for the President is the attitude of the Republican leadership—an attitude shared generally by the economically conservative Southern Democrats.</br></br>The Republicans contend that Mr. Kennedy has overstated the economic situation for political reasons, and therefore they refuse to go along with calls for hurry. “We do not believe this is the time to push the panic button,” Senator Dirksen said last week.

text: Tire stock market reverted yesterday to the type of performance that was common during the early part of this year. The word for it is “churning.”</br></br>Although trading was heavy, prices on the New York Stock Exchange closed down slightly on average. There was no clear-cut pattern in the market, either of advance or decline.</br></br>There was some disappointment—but not surprise—in Wall Street over the market’s failure to continue last week's strong advance. Last week prices scored the best gain for a week in six months. However, on technical grounds alone some readjustment had been expected and that was largely the story yesterday.</br></br>The analysts and the observers, almost to a man, remained convinced that stocks were in time headed for new highs, that the bullish influence would not be denied. This comment by a major brokerage house expressed the majority view: “The vigor with which seasoned equities rebounded last week from a brief corrective action demonstrated * * * that stock prices probably still had further to go before culmination of the sustained advance beginning last autumn."</br></br>“Instead of highly speculative ‘magic’ stocks dominating the current trend, the movement is more selective and the better quality securities are making the more favorable showing — always a healthy sign.” This was not to say that speculation as a factor had disappeared from the market. text: The declines in stock and bond prices in recent weeks are spreading the idea along Main Street that the postwar inflation is over and that business enterprise and the national economy must get used to living in a world of stable money values and unflagging competition.</br></br>This view has been held in Wall Street for a much longer time, but not without reservations. The reservations of the financial professional stem from the increasing vogue in economic discussions for confusing the inflation malady with its symptoms. Inflation is a disease of the money supply. Inflation is an excessive amount of money in active circulation. A major symptom of the inflation malady is rising prices.</br></br>Thus, when the financial specialist hears it insinuated by public officials that rising prices either constitute or cause inflation, the professionals are spurred to suspect that the news of the death of inflation, like the legendary passing of the undefunct Mark Twain, may be somewhat premature.</br></br>Indeed, rising prices, instead of abetting inflation, tend to restrain the malady, or even to entrain its opposite—deflation. If the supply of money is not increased, the higher priced, but unenlarged, supply of goods and services would in time press</br></br>The big related question is: How will the deficit be financed ? Will the Treasury borrow from the banking system? If so. to what extent will the Federal Reserve System make the money available by increasing the reserves of the commercial banks? And, if the Federal Reserve thus causes the money supply to be swelled to accommodate the Treasury, will the central bank thereafter move to shrink the money supply back to the status quo ante?

text: If the stock market decline is a “riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma,” then today’s unsure bond market must be a “myth wrapped in a clichS inside a complexity."</br></br>Bond men thus garbled facetiously last week the diction of Winston Churchill and President Kennedy as they pondered why high-grade bonds did not keep rising in price in orthodox accompaniment to the 1962 stock market’s major secondary slide.</br></br>In capitalist folklore, the bond market should go up when the stock market goes down. Forces that make for rising stock prices —business expansion and big borrowing from the banks and the public—tend to use up the money supply. The intensified bidding for debt capital causes the prices of bonds to rise.</br></br>On the other hand, forces that cause stock prices to go down— a decline in business activity and a donline in borrowing from the banks and the public—generally tend to malke bond prices rise, because surplus investment funds are forced to compete for the purchase of a dwindling supply of bond issues.</br></br>True, the sharp stock sell-off of May 28 was accompanied, by the dumping of bonds, but this was viewed as only a momentary affair, dictated by the need of investment houses and individual investors to improve cash liquidity in the wake of the drastic overnight shrinkage in equity values. .

text: By ARTHUR KROCK WASHINGTON, May 4—The fiscal philosophy of the Kennedy Administration—that the best method of reducing unemployment and increasing the gross national product is a simultaneous combination of tax cuts and more Federal spending—was already mixed up when Secretary of the Treasury Dillon addressed the Chamber of Commerce here this week. By the end of his speech this fiscal philosophy was whirling even faster in the mixer.</br></br>In January, the Secretary had stigmatized as “unrealistic” the arguments of many economists and industrialists that the need for a tax cut was not. as the President and .he were insisting, to avert a for another combination to start the economy on a steady march toward higher levels. This proposed dual program was a tax cut, in company with reduced Federal spending which would reduce the prospective deficit for fiscal '64.</br></br>In May, when Dillon spoke to the Chamber, the first of these arguments had already been sustained by the facts. Not only was there no recession, but economic conditions had improved on their own, since Congress meanwhile has done nothing about cutting taxes. But, even though Dillon—by holding out the hope that new revenues created by the economic improvement would, despite a concurrent tax cut, permit the reduction of the prospective '64 deficit from $12 to $11 billions— conceded "reality” to this proof of a forecast he had found "unrealistic” four months previously, he continued to find "unrealism” in the argument that there should be a simultaneous slash in Federal spending.</br></br>(2) The danger is not fanciful because "President Kennedy was very close to launching . . . this new mythology when, in speaking April 19 ... to the American Society of Newspaper Editors in Washington, he asserted that 'a cut of $5,000,000,000 now from the proposed Federal budget... would cause 1,000,000 fewer jobs’ ” by the end of fiscal '64.</br></br>(3) In supporting his estimate, Mr. Kennedy "assigned a great part of the responsibility for the 1957-58 recession to what he described as the “tremendous drop in 1957 of Federal purchases, in the defense area particularly, and credited it with having added to the miseries caused by what he apparently believes to have been a generally mistaken fiscal and monetary policy—namely a $12,-500,000 deficit in 1959, the largest outflow in a period of years of gold and dollars amounting to nearly $12,000,000,000, and a recession in 1960.”

text: The continuing importance of flexible monetary policy — and changes in interest rates— was underlined in a speech last week by Per Jacobsson, head of the International Monetary Fund.</br></br>Mr. Jacobsson, who is one of the major architects of the world’s monetary network, made clear that monetary policy should not be put into mothballs because of the new emphasis of fiscal — or tax — policy. In his view, the Federal Reserve in the United States and central banks abroad still have a big role to play.</br></br>He ds opposed to following the orthodox remedy of utilizing tighter money and higher interest rates in order to cope with the deficit in our balance of payments. Instead, he thinks that European central banks can discourage an outflow of dollars from the United States by easing money and reducing interest rates.</br></br>on the surface, Mr. Jacobsson may appear to be a cheap money enthusiast. But this is not the case. Rather, he can be classified as a monetary activist in contrast to those who think that monetary policy, under present conditions, should be relegated to a passive or defensive role.</br></br>In recent weeks, the Federal Reserve has adopted a policy characterized as "less easy,” and which is aimed at stemming the outflow of dollars. As one economist after another has remarked, getting there was easy once we finally began to use the tools that have always been available, but staying there without serious difficulties is something else again.</br></br>The prosperity itself is so evident one can almost smell it — unemployment down to 4 per.cent of the labor force, profits up 20 per cent last year, factory workers' earnings up by one-quarter in five years, records tumbling on every side. Last year more than two million families crossed over the poverty line, achieving an annual income of $3,000 or better, and the unemployment rate among Negro adults has dropped to 5.5 per cent. Not only can we all feel and sec the prosperity, we naturally enjoy it But what about sustaining it? Government policy played a major role in getting us there: can it keep us there?</br></br>Just as explorers may argue among themselves over the next step to take as new ground is encountered, so the entry of the American economy into the new territory of near-full employment has already stirred the briskest economic debate In years. text: CIVIL rights, the war in Vietnam, inflation and taxes— these are minor problems compared to one which millions of American parents are now facing, that of helping their children learn the “new mathematics." The problem isn't made any easier by the fact that the stores are currently displaying a dozen paperback books about mathematics whose covers suggest, somewhat misleadingly, that they will provide first aid to the perplexed. As a matter of fact, only six of the books are of value to parents, and these only with qualifications.</br></br>Before assessing their individual merits, it would be well to consider just what the new mathematics is and why it was introduced into school curricula.</br></br>For many years there had been rather general agreement that the teaching of mathematics was unsuccessful. The standard explanation of this failure is that the traditional curriculum taught only what was known before 1700 while from that date to 1955 mathematics had changed as much as had physics, chemistry and biology. (The implication is that students knew of these purported changes and refused to take an interest in the antiquated material.) At any rate, early in the 1950's a number of mathematicians and teachers decided that the curriculum was at fault and had to be refashioned.</br></br>Beginning in 1952, one new curriculum was fashioned by the University of Illinois Committee on School Mathematics. In 1954 the Commission on Mathematics of the College Entrance Examination Board started a campaign for adoption of the new mathematics. After 1957, assisted with grants from foundations and governmental agencies whose purses seem to have been loosened by the advent of Sputnik, a dozen other projects, dominated by college professors, produced their versions of new curricula. Of these projects the most influential is the School Mathematics Study Group, established by the American Mathematical Society, the organization of mathematicians concerned with research. The new curricula were at first directed toward the reform of high-school mathematics courses but soon afterward were extended to include the elementary Schools.</br></br>One could challenge the conclusion that the failure of mathematics education in the past was due to the poor cur- riculum. One may have doubts —as I do—about the panacea qualities of the new math. Nevertheless, it is now a fact of American educational life, and for better or for worse, a legal precondition of parenthood; many a modem parent must face the prospect of helping his children cope with it, for help they do need.

text: Most economists have long argued that the Government’s guide-posts for keeping prices stable and checking excessive wage increases, if they had any effect at all, would break down at a time when the economy moved to full employment and a condition of exuberant or excess demand. The President emphasized that the inflation has been very modest by comparison with other countries and also by comparison with previous periods of price increases in this country.</br></br>The second was that there are some elements in the outlook that indicate a lessening of inflationary pressure in the future. text: The President’s Council of Economic Advisers has held out an attractive prospect. text: By M. J. KOSSANT Is it or isn’t it ? Business forecasters pondering whether the economy is in a recession have been unable to reach a consensus. Forecasters should know by now what kind of ’pattern will prevail for the rest of 1967. After all, the results of the first two months are already in and it should not be overly difficult to figure out what happens next.</br></br>But forecasters appear to be in agreement only in observing that the economy is experiencing a definite slowdown in business activity. They are at odds over whether this current pause will be followed by a fresh upsurge or a further decline.</br></br>This dispute over the outlook is renewed proof that business forecasting remains an imprecise art rather than a precise science. It also emphasizes the special difficulty in determining economic turning points— those critical periods when activity undergoes decisive change.</br></br>But whether or not the economy is at a turning point now, most forecasters are sufficiently disturbed by what has been happening to business activity to question the need for tax increases called for by the Johnson Administration, Even those who believe the slowdown will soon come to an end do not think that the ensuing rise will be vigorous enough to warrant curbing demand through an increased tax on individual and corporate incomes.</br></br>In taking this position, forecasters are not only suggesting that it is a mistake to formulate economic policy too far in advance of actual developments, they also are saying that the whole idea of managing the economy through the “fine tuning" of monetary and fiscal instruments is unlikely to work during the most critical periods if forecasters cannot decide with assurance whether a turning point is at hand.

text: The following article was written by James J. O’Leary, executive vice president and economist for the United States Trust Company of New York.</br></br>noted that the Nixon Administration and the Federal Reserve authorities recognized that the expectation of continuing inflation had become a powerful destabilizing force in our economy, and that fiscal and monetary restraints were being directed to dampen down the widespread belief that a persistent high rate of inflation was inevitable. The purpose or tms article is to examine how we stand today in our efforts to combat the expectation of inflation — how much progress, if any, has been made toward cooling it.</br></br>The expectation of inflation is the conviction widely shared by investors, corporate planners, labor leaders, consumers, public officials and the public at large that, for the foreseeable future, the general price level of the United States is likely to continue to rise at a very high rate by any historical standards. This expectation has, of course, been nurtured by the accelerating rate of in-'' crease in prices during much of the past four and one-half years. It is based to a large degree today on the belief that the wage - price spiral cannot be broken by fiscal and monetary restraints so long as the Government is unwilling to tolerate more than a moderate and shortlived increase of unemployment.</br></br>As the expectation of inflation has built up since mid-1965, it has had a profound effect upon decision-makers in our economy. It has made investors unwilling to buy straight bonds and mortgages except at very high interest rates—and it has thus built an “inflation premium” into long-term interest rates. The belief that the cost of capital projects will continue to rise at a rapid rate provides part of the explanation for the surprisingly high rate of capital spending.</br></br>Organized labor is seeking in its bargaining not only to catch up with past rises in the cost of living but also to anticipate sizable increases in the future. State and local government capital projects are being pressed in the present to avoid the higher costs expected in the future. Burns, chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, suggested today 11 possible additional steps that might be taken by the Government to help slow inflation as the economy expands.</br></br>These ranged up to compulsory arbitration of some major labor disputes and a new “price and wage review board” that would not have mandatory powers.</br></br>Mr. Burns, whose agency governs the growth of the nation’s money and credit, was not specific on monetary policy. text: The drive of the Nixon Administration to swing the United States’ balance of payments from deficit to surplus is running into a serious obstacle—rising unemployment in Europe and Japan. Although the slump abroad had begun before President Nixon’s Aug. 15 actions in floating the dollar and imposing the 10 per cent import tax, the American trade and monetary moves are coming under heavy fire for aggravating what many businessmen and Government officials abroad now fear may become a major recession.</br></br>Under pressure from their domestic industries, foreign governments arc likely to resist letting Iheir currencies float higher against the dollar.</br></br>If unemployment continues to increase overseas and world trade should decline, there could be a more decisive breakdown in the international monetary system than has occurred.</br></br>The effect on world trade and development would be grave. The business decline of 1929-30, which for more than a year seemed like a characteristic cyclical downturn, was turned into the most serious world depression in history bv the collapse of the inter-r.ional monetary system. There is danger today that</br></br>the non-Communist world, which since the end of World War II has been led by the United States, may split into isolated and protectionist blocs. text: WASHINGTON—Prior to Aug. 15, 1971, the Administration’s economic policy was one of benign neglect. Instead, it produced both 6 per cent unemployment and 6 per cent inflation.</br></br>Abroad, the policy was to consider the dollar invincible. .Foreign central banks would continue to accept endless dollar deficits, no matter how badly over-valued the dollar was. No fundamental realignment of currencies,</br></br>But then came Aug. 15 and the New Economic Policy which the President has encumbered with obeisances to the false gods of trickle-down at home and protectionism abroad.</br></br>At home, the price-wage freeze was accompanied by a tax-reduction program which has now been substantially enacted by the Congress. In essence, the tax program gives corporations and their stockholders an $S-billion a year annual tax reduction mainly through the 7 per cent investment tax credit and rapid depreciation. After the first year, the tax (1) By obviously discriminating against the wage earner, it destroys the social contract upon which effective wage-price controls must be founded. Labor’s increasing unwillingness to go along with meaningful wage restraints is due in large measure to the inequality of sacrifice brought about by the tax bill.</br></br>(2) The nation’s "fiscal dividend,” out of which was to be paid the cost of health and education and environmental control and revenue-sharing in the decade of the seventies, has been effectively wiped out by the permanent fracturing of the revenues implicit in the tax-reduction bill.

text: Productivity gains are not a certain cure for all the problems afflicting the American economy. text: A price and wage freeze stops an inflation in its tracks,. But any freeze, even if completely effective, must soon give way to a Phase Two which restores some of the flexibility that the economy needs to be able to adjust to continually changing conditions. This means permitting some wages and prices to rise relatively to other wages and prices.</br></br>The Administration has been criticized for vagueness in the "details” of the proposed adjustments, but it is really the principles that still need to be established. The basic principles required for stability, flexibility and fairness are really simple and straightforward.</br></br>(1) Stability. Since productivity can be expected to continue to rise at about 3 per cent per annum, wages can, and must, rise at 3 per cent relative, to prices. For absolute stability of the average price level the average wage must rise at just 3 per cent per annum. If we aim only at holding inflation to 2 per cent, average wages must rise at 5 per cent.</br></br>(2) Flexibility. Wages must rise more than the average in areas where labor has become exceptionally scarce, so as to induce workers to move into these areas. Where unemployment is, say, less than half the national average, wages should rise at, say, 8 per cent if the average rate of increase of wages is to be 5 per cent. In the opposite case, where unemployment is exceptionally high, say more than twice the national average, the wage will have to rise less than the average— say at 2 per cent—so as to induce labor to keep out or to leave for where labor is scarcer.</br></br>(3) Fairness. The resulting changes in relative costs and prices will induce consumers to shift their demand from the products of areas with low unemployment to the products of areas with heavy unemployment. The exceptionally high wage increases will occur where conditions are below average—which is why there are so few workers there in relation to the number of jobs available.

text: DETROIT—Many proposals to combat inflation have an Alice in Wonderland flavor. While avowedly aimed at price increases, they direct their fire at wage increases.</br></br>The absurdity is all the more bizarre in the light of the facts on price and wage movements. In the three most recent inflations (including the present) prices started upward when unit labor costs were actually falling. Labor costs began their rise later, as workers sought to catch up with prior inflation. Similarly, wage increases tend to recede toward rates approximating productivity growth as price rises abate. Although wage restraint does not induce price restraint the reverse is true.</br></br>Nevertheless, proposals confusing effects with causes continue to gain reverential consideration. The latest of the genre is the Wallich-Weintraub proposal to impose an extra, penalty tax on the profits of corporations for granting wage increases in excess of a specified guidepost, no matter how justifiably—but not for raising prices, no matter how unjustifiably.</br></br>Nothing in the proposal would prevent the kind of double-cross U.S. Steel attempted in 1962. A corporation using the “anti-inflationary" tax as an excuse to obtain a bargain-basement union contract, binding on its workers for 3 years, could announce a wholly unwarranted price boost the following day without any penalty whatsoever.</br></br>If the proposal actually restrained wage increases, it would unfairly impose the sacrifices of combatting inflation upon workers, who did not cause it and are already among its chief victims. Wage increases are larger than normal today because of the need of workers to protect living standards against inflation and to avoid distortion of the income distribution to their disadvantage.

Sharp variations in monetary conditions have high and frequently underestimated costs. If our economic stabilization objectives could be achieved with more stable monetary conditions in the future, we would all be better off.</br></br>2. In an attempt, primarily, to offset extremely inflationary and erratic spending policies of the Government and large businesses, monetary policy and conditions here varied drastically and expensively. Political debates and pressures on the Federal Reserve have always been prominent. Within reason this is proper, but recently they have been increasing unreasonably. Once normal inventory accumulation starts, the pace could well quicken. Buying by consumers, spending by governments, investment by business in plant and equipment and construction of housing are all advancing strongly.</br></br>• Reflecting the quicker pace of business, higher earnings in the first quarter—sometimes sharply higher— were reported by numerous corporations, after a long period when profits, by some measures, were at a quarter-century low.</br></br>• The first quarter saw the expected post-freeze ‘'bulge" in prices, but the rise in consumer prices, at least, moderated in March. The world is in for trouble, political as well as economic, and someone better "do something." But that •JThe first, as much a political as an economic criticism, is exemplified by Fred Borgsten, a former assistant to I-Ienry Kissinger, assistant to the President for National Security Affairs, under President Nixon. It is that the United States should be moving much faster in getting negotiations going on longer-term world monetary reform. The danger seen is that delay will bring a divided monetary and political world, with tho Europeans in particular moving toward a controlled and "inward-looking” system of their own, with many restrictions on tho free flow of goods and money.</br></br>*JThc second, identified with Edward M. text: WASHINGTON—More than 10 mil* lion workers were exempted from the wage-price controls program last week, bringing the total in this group to 32.5 million—56 per cent of the nonfarm, nongovernment labor force. These unions, by and large, remain subject to Pay Board authority. Most of their members earn more than $2.75 ah hour, which is the new minimum wage subject to Pay Board jurisdiction. All workers earning less are now exempt.</br></br>• The Cost of Living Council, which oversees the controls program, announced the $2.75 standard last week after a Federal court here ruled that the council’s earlier figure of $1.90 was less than Congress intended.</br></br>Workers earning less than $2.75 are unlikely to start a round of inflationary settlements, officials said. Such workers are employed largely in in- dustries that are substantially unorganized, notably wholesale and retail trade, finance and other services. As one Government economist put it, “there is a plentiful supply of those workers—which has tended to keep their wages down.”</br></br>There is one risk, however, in having more than half the labor force exempt: a greater potential for an upward creep in nonunion wages if unemployment moves below 5 per cent. text: Steel stocks repeatedly have disappointed investors in recent years. Whether the laggard steels will find favor remains, of course, to be seen. text: WASHINGTON—During March, Government reports disclosed last week, American consumers experienced the worst rate of inflation in nearly a quarter century—a major worsening of an illness that had shown distinct Improvement in 1971 and 1972.</br></br>But at the same time, as other reports revealed, the boom in the economy—a major cause of the rising prices—produced some good news too. First the bad news, most of it signaled in advance by earlier statistics: • Dominated once again by food prices, the Consumer Price Index rose by eight-tenths of I per cent in March, bringing the annual inflation rate for the first quarter to 8.8 per cent—the highest since the Korean War in 1951. Food prices alone rose in the first quarter at the extraordinary</br></br>annual rate of 30 per cent. President Nixon’s goal is an inflation rate for consumer prices as a whole of only 2.5 per cent by the end of the year, though he had set no specific goal for the first quarter. • Another measure of Inflation— the price index for the Gross National Product—rose at a 6 per cent annual rate in the first quarter, double last year’s inflation.</br></br>While the shift to the less mandatory Phase 3 system of price and wage controls undoubtedly played a part in the sudden jump in the inflation rate, the underlying cause seems to be the boom, which has now brought the nation’s output close to its capacity, of plant if not of labor.</br></br>• Consumer incomes on an annual basis crossed the triliion-dollar mapk in March for the first time, up an enormous $90-biilion, 10 per cent, from a year earlier. People clearly have the money to pay the higher prices, and retail sales in the first quarter run about 15 per cent ahead of last year.

text: WASHINGTON, April 27— Despite another strong rise in productivity in the first quarter and unusually small wage increases negotiated by unions during the period, unit labor costs in the United States rose at more than triple the rate of last year, the Labor Department reported today.</br></br>The chief explanation for the seeming paradox, the report indicated, was the big jump in the employer share of social security taxes that began Jan. 1 [along with the parallel increase in the tax paid by employes.</br></br>Thus, from the point of view of labor, wages rose only mod-icstly but from the point of view of employers the cost of each 'man-hour worked rose fairly sharply. Today’s report was the first clear evidence of the inflationary impact of the huge increase in social security benefits and taxes that swept through Congress last year with almost no opposition.</br></br>^Productivity, or output per man-hour, in the entire private economy rose at an annual rate of 4.7 per cent in the first quarter, well above the historical average and a little better than last year’s strong productivity growth of 4.2 per cent. •jFirst-ycar wage increases in 138 “major” collective bargaining settlements—those affecting at least 1,000 workers —in the first quarter averaged only 5.3 per cent, well witnin the Government’s guidelines and sharply less than the average first-year increase of 7 per cent in settlements reached in bargaining last year.</br></br>tJDespite these moderate un-jion settlements, average compensation paid by employers for each man-hour worked rose at an annual rate of 11.7 per jeent in the first quarter, well above the 7.9 per cent of the fourth quarter of last year and the 6.2 per cent for 1972 as a whole.

text: SLATER, Mo., March 29-Round steak was bringing $1.79 a pound today at the U. S. Supermarket, about 50 cents more than at the turn of the year. But no one complained to Mrs. Betty Moore, the checkout worker, who stood beneath a sign urging customers to “fight inflation.” No irate housewives picketed on Main Street. There was no demand for horse meat.</br></br>This is a farm town, one of those heart-of-America collections of white frame houses, squat brick stores and jutting wheat elevators, home for 2,600 people whose standard of living rises and falls with the rise and fall of cattle and grain prices.</br></br>Like the farmers who raise the rich yellow com and fat slaughter steers in the surrounding fields, the town is enjoying inflation.</br></br>“Sure my grocery bill has increased, but you don't complain these days when you live in a farm town,” Miss Valda Coleman, a secretary, said.</br></br>Deposits in the shiny steel vault at the State Bank of Slater have jumped 20 per cent in the last 12 months.

text: The research department at Bache & Co. felt the stock market was ripe for an upturn a few weeks ago, so Joseph Cucuzza, Bache’s chief technical analyst^ flashed an intermediate-term buy signal over the firm’s wire system.</br></br>As soon as he read the wire, William J. Alpern, a registered representative with a sense of humor in Bache’s Chrysler Building office in New York, called the analyst on the telephone and quipped: “All right, just send me two carloads of intermediate-term buyers.” • Therein lies Wall Street’s chief problem today: not enough buyers. The average investor has been alienated. Despite clear evidence of a strong recovery in the national economy, he’s still not buying stocks.</br></br>The result is another financial squeeze in the securities industry. The profits of most brokerage and investment banking firms are in a downtrend and many firms are understood to have operated with deficits in the first quarter.</br></br>While the situation has not reached crisis proportions, it’s worrying just about everybody in Wall Street. The result is a widespread epidemic of malaise that evokes memories of the bear market of 1969-70.</br></br>Large financial institutions are increasingly dominating the trading in stocks. The little guy, on the other hand, feels he is being squeezed out of the market by institutional swingers and by escalating brokerage charges. So he’s not trading, and his absence has drained the market of the vitality it used to have.

text: Sol Siedman is a 55-year-old small businessman who imports watchmakers’ and jewelers’ supplies and tools and who says he earns less than $15,000 a year. He sometimes plays the stock market At least he used to.</br></br>Mr. Siedman was a customer of now-defunct Weis Securities, Inc. He had done very well in the market, running a relatively small amount of money into a fortune worth at one time more than $l-million.</br></br>Like many . substantial Weis customers, Mr. Siedman was notified weeks before the firm went into liquidation that Weis could not handle accounts with such large debit balances as his. He owed $350,000 on margin.</br></br>Weis, at the New York Stock Exchange’s suggestion, was attempting to head off insolvency by eliminating accounts like Mr. Siedman’s. A firm borrows to finance its customers’ margin debt, thus adding to its debt.</br></br>The elimination of a relatively few large accounts can have a dramatic effect on a firm’s debt structure. In Weis’s case, however, the maneuver didn’t do the trick. On May 24, the firm failed.

text: Up, up and away the prices go. text: The President considers it the nation’s “No. 1 problem”—a judgment in which he is joined by journalists, politicians, business commentators and virtually every housewife. That inflation has been an economic disaster is part of the conventional wisdom, subscribed to even by economists who ought to know better.</br></br>The fact is that detailed examinations of the impact of the last two decades’ inflation upon Americans have been few and far between. We know all about the manner in which inflated supermarket prices can eat away last year’s pay raise. And the Nixon Administration’s ill-starred efforts to halt inflation are all too familiar—culminating</br></br>James W. Kuhn, a professor at the Columbia Graduate School of Business, teaches and writes in the fields of economics, public policy and labor.</br></br>a fortnight ago in a Phase 4 that makes not even a pretense of stopping the upward swing in the months ahead. What the general public does not realize has been summed up very well by Paul W. McCracken, former chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers and a formulator of the Nixon game plan to slow “runaway inflation.” There is, he says, an “almost total absence of solid and extensive empirical studies about the effects of inflation.” Recently, however, several economic studies have begun to give us some clues. As yet we are limited to analyses of broad categories of people and economic units, and the complexity of the data is such that initial conclusions must be tentative. But their tendency is unmistakable: Inflation has not been the disaster we have imagined it to be. In the words of Stanford University professor G. L. Bach, “the American economy has become to a larger extent than is generally realized an income-adjusting economy.” day - to - supermarket - day, most Americans have come through the inflation of the past two decades quite well. Wage-earners have gained. Most of the elderly have kept up with price rises. The wealthy have lost on some counts and won on others.</br></br>Rampant inflation, of the kind that ravaged Germany in the twenties, would of course produce a very different result. But we have been experiencing something else. Since 1950, the broadest measure of change in the price level (the Gross National Product deflator) indicates an average annual increase of 2.84 per cent; since 1965, a yearly increase of 4.22 per cent; during the past year, 3.41 per cent. By any definition, this has not been rampant. Professor Bach, in the title of a recent study, calls it “The New Inflation.” And the new inflation’s effects upon major groups of Americans flies in the face of the conventional wisdom.

text: WASHINGTON, Oct. 8—President Ford has now defined the economic crisis of the nation and proposed a catalogue of remedies. The question now is whether the solutions he proposed are equal to the crisis he defined, and the fear here is that he didn’t bite the bullet but nibbled it.</br></br>In these abnormal times, and especially a month before the mid-year Congressional elections, he put forward some unpopular and politically bold proposals, but the whole thrust of his speech to the Congress was that the nation was in mortal danger, and he asked that we mutually pledge to each other, not “our lives, our fortunes, and our sacred honor," but our comfort, our support, and 5 per cent of our gas and oil.</br></br>It would be hard to overemphasize the relief in Washington to find a President stating, with the utmost sincerity, his belief about what had to be done in the interests of the Republic. And for the first time in years, to see a Congress that accepts him at his word, without doubting his motives.</br></br>Still, his proposals, honest and sensible as they were, scarcely measure up to the spectacular menace and danger he put before the Congress. Inflation was as bad as war, he suggested, while refusing to call for a declaration of war. “We have had enough early warnings,” he said. . . The time to intercept [the enemy inflation] is almost gone.” But he didn’t intercept it.</br></br>"I say to you with all sincerity,” Mr. Ford remarked in the peroration of his speech, “that inflation, our present public enemy, will — unless it is whipped — destroy our country, our homes, our liberties, our property, and finally our national pride —as surely as any well-armed wartime enemy.”

text: WINTER is still almost two months away, but it has already arrived on the economic scene—and is becoming more chilling with each passing day. McCracken of the University of Michigan, said last week for the Administration to refrain from ‘‘calling a spade a spade" and publically recognizing that the sixth recession since the end of World War II is upon the nation.</br></br>Secretary of Commerce Frederick U. Dent has persisted in maintaining that the economic downturn that started late last year is merely a “sideways waffle.” Others in the Administration have also tended to minimize the business slump, much the way the Nixon men kept referring to the 1969-70 recession as only “a rolling readjustment.” But it is significant that Arthur F. text: The old axiom that you can’t beat lomething with nothing will be sorely tested as the demise of wage and prica controls approaches April 30. Although director controls now have fewer public supporters than streaking, they did serve to demonstrate at least a resolve to beat inflation. After' rising gently through most" of 1974, the number of jobs dropped by about 800,000 last month.</br></br>The unemployment rate of 6.5 per cent was the highest for a month since October, 1961. It is widely believed that the rate will go higher in the months ahead. In August, it was 5.4 per cent. In November, there were just under 6 million unemployed, up 1.1 million in three months.</br></br>Additional layoffs in the automobile and several other industries, and some related to the coal strike, have been announced since the mid-November job survey.</br></br>Ron Nessen, the White House press secretary, said that the rise in unemployment “is a source of great concern." text: Barely seven months after Wage-price controls were dropped from the economic game plan they are again receiving serious attention in the debate over a strategy to beat inflation and recession. As time runs out, there is a rising probability that controls will make a comeback because the bench has been emptied of other alternatives.</br></br>Mike Mansfield, the Senate majority leader, has consistently expressed strong support for controls and he has now been joined by Speaker of the House Carl Albert and other Democratic leaders. Recent, polls reveal that a majority of Americans now favors the reimposition of some form of controls.</br></br>The renewed popularity of controls is striking in -view of the sour experience with government restraints on wages and prices. After apparent success during Phase I and II, prices rose rapidly during Phases III and IV, and the Nixon stabilization program ended with a bang from the price index and whimpers by the consumer. Consequently, controls lost their economic credibility and political appeal and Congress quietly buried the program in legislative Boot Hill.</br></br>The revival of interest in controls reflects the sheer magnitude of the current inflation, the impatience with or disbelief in the remedies prescribed by the Ford Administration, and the perils of dealing with inflation and recession concurently.</br></br>As President Ford indicated this week, the Administration is still committed to budgetary and monetary restraint in coping with inflation. This approach has inherent political deficiencies.

text: Last Thursday President Nixon opened a "national dialogue” on how to cope with inflation. He invited 31 businessmen and economists to discuss with him the worldwide disease that has been plaguing ordinary citizens and national economies, threatening political leaders and shredding the reputations of pundits whose remedies don't seem to work.</br></br>The New York Times conducted its own sampling of opinion among businessmen, economists and representatives of labor and the consumer. They were asked, "What recommendations would you make for dealing with our inflation-prone economy?”</br></br>There seems to be a consensus that inflation is a serious illness and probably not susceptible to cure. Perhaps, like alcoholism, it may only be controllable and then through enormous exercise of will and self-discipline.</br></br>At all stages of the spectrum, there is recognition of the political elements in both the causes and suggested prescriptions for inflation. Capital investment to spur production and mitigate inflationary scarcities of goods and commodities was repeatedly cited.</br></br>There are no quick answers to today’s inflation. Moreover, any solutions must now be both multinational and national and encompass critical attention to political, psychological and social as well as economic forces.
