text: After two years of abort rations, trade unions are demanding and winning larger slices of the pie at the bargaining table. With consumer prices climbing at more than 10 per cent per year, organized labor Is hurrying to catch up and to build some protection against future Inflation. At the same time, the dismantling of wage-price controls has removed any legal restraints on union demands. Under these circumstances, it is not surprising that labor has rediscovered Samuel Gompers’s admonition to seek "more, more, here and now."</br></br>This renewed labor militancy Is sure to complicate the task of restoring price stability to the economy. Wage increases that outrun gains in productivity will exert further leverage On prices. In addition, generous wage settlements help to sustain the expectations that feed inflation. On the other hand the unions’ claims have a strong ring of equity in making their members whole for past economic losses. There is no obvious or easy way out of this dilemma.</br></br>The origins of this situation are readily apparent For nearly three years, trade union behavior was orchestrated by cues from the Government. However, while unions generally respected the spirit if not the letter, of the old Pay Board standard limiting annual wage gains to 5.5 per cent prices soared at a double-digit rate by the beginning of 1974. As a result, the purchasing power of the average worker’s weekly take-home pay dipped by 4.6 per cent in the last 12 months.</br></br>With the expiratioh of controls, union leaders have moved to rectify this imbalance. The East Coast longshoremen’s union recently negotiated a 31 per cent wage increase over a three-year period. In San Francisco, the plumbers won an 18 per cent pay hike for one year, raising the hourly rate to $15.20—a figure associated more with airline pilots than with leaky faucets. Even In the men’s clothing industry, where the union traditionally has been wary of wage competition from non-union firms, the Amalgamated Clothing Workers won an estimated 30 per cent pay Increase for three years. Over-all, a 10 per cent wage gain has become an accepted target for union negotiators.</br></br>Unions also have pressed for protection against future erosion of real earnings. Like many businessmen, labor leaders were not sure whether the upsurge of prices that began in early 1973 was a passing indisposition or the beginning of a prolonged ailment. As it became apparent that the economy was In for an extended siege of inflation, these expectations have been reflected in union demands at the bargaining table.

text: IT seemed appropriate, five years ago at this time, when the glow of the Soaring Sixties was diminishing and a new decade was starting with the United States in the midst of its worst inflation in 19 years, to recall the words of Thomas Paine: "These are the times that try men’s souls.”</br></br>That historic rallying pronouncement, delivered to the American colonists in their fight for freedom, seemed fitting in January, 1970, when the United States was struggling to extricate itself from the excesses of the previous five' years. And it seems even more suitable now on the virtual eve of the nation’s bicentennial.</br></br>Despite its amazing evolution from 13 disparate and fragile colonies into the world’s mightiest nation, endowed with immense natural .resources and the heritage of imaginative, diligent and creative people, this country is now facing an economic crisis that some fear threatens its fantastic achievements and the very system that helped to fashion them.</br></br>These worries appear excessive—and they are not widely held. The nation does not seem to. be even close to the brink of an economic collapse similar to the disaster of the Great Depression of the nineteen-thirties. But there is validity to the wide concern that the current stagnation will degenerate into the worst of the six recessions that have afflicted the United States since World War II.</br></br>Few would question the statement that the United States has just emerged from one of its most dramatic and painful years—one that was worse in many respects than the tragic periods of the recent past: the Cuban missile confrontation in 1962, the assassination of President John F. Kennedy the following year, the long and draining Vietnam war from the mid-sixties until 1972, the civil-rights tensions and other crises of the last decade and a half.

text: Cities are built and unbuilt by the forces of law and economics, supply and demand, cash flow and the bottom line, far more than by the ideals, intentions, talents and visions of architects and planners. Right now, the conventional wisdom about investment construction—tear down the old and put up the new for maximum return on the land—is taking a beating. And so are cities, in terms of some of the things that the real estate recession is doing to the urban environment.</br></br>In New York, in particular, with tight money, inflation, cost overruns and a decade of commercial overbuilding, the traditional development pattern has bombed out. And so have a dismaying number of big new buildings. In an almost unprecedented situation, paralleled only by the great depression, completed skyscrapers stand empty or near-empty, deep in the red. Eerily silent sites attest to the fact that construction has stopped on important buildings.</br></br>Costs have escalated beyond the possibility of satisfactory returns, and the money—in a business where virtually every penny is borrowed—has run out. Crisis has quietly turned into catastrophe, and not the least effect is the damage being done to the city itself.</br></br>The most cautionary tale comes from Chicago, where nothing could illustrate the problem more forcefully than the story of the Old Stock Exchange. In a casebook adherence to investment practice, Adler and Sullivan’s landmark structure in Chicago's Loop was demolished for new construction in 1971. Critics and preservationists bled profusely in print before it came down, and even New York’s Metropolitan Museum lusted after the 76-year-old Sullivan terra cotta ornament and rusticated ground floor arcades. Arguments about quality, style and the Chicago htritag* were to no avail. The fate of the building, which stood on prime commercial land, was sealed with the statement that it was "economically unviable.”</br></br>And so it was bulldozed, and a 43-story glass and steel replacement, called the Heller International Building, went up at 30 North LaSalle, backed by astute investors undeterred by art or sentimentality or anything but the higher truths of the real estate process. Sound business practice, as defined and revered by the development community, prevailed.

text: Many plans have been advanced to get the unemployed back to work sooner than the Ford Administration’s programs nnw envisage. All run up against a common objection —they presume sharply higher Government spending (or its equivalent, the forgoing of tax revenues), raising the specter of reinvigorated inflation.</br></br>The trouble lies In what might be called the macro-economic blind spot. Planners have focused on the number of dollars spent almost without regard to whether the dollars are spent to maximum effect toward the reduction of unemployment.</br></br>It would be hard to find a more apt or ironic example of the blind spot than unemployment insurance itself. State and Federal governments spend, and must go on spending as long as unemployment stays high, billions ol dollars to sustain the millions of Americans out of work. The money definitely relieves personal hardships that might otherwise cause grave social unrest—no mean accomplishment. But the huge sums do little if anything to attack the economic causes of hardship. History explains why.</br></br>Unemployment insurance evolved at about the same time as the old Agricultural Administration, at the depth of the Depression, and it manifested a similar philosophy. Both sought to mitigate the ravages of competition by paying the unfortunate to withhold resources from the market.</br></br>Farmers were compensated to keep their land fallow. The unemployed were and are paid not to work—not to add to the nation's stock of goods and services. But wouldn’t the unemployed benefit much more if the money' went instead to employers as an inducement to hire the jobless quickly, without further inflation? costs—when higher sales volume cannot be met by existing staff, for example. Hence Government spending to increase aggregate demand and sales. But the equation runs the otner way, too. If the cost of an additional employe diminishes, so does the value he must produce to justify his hire.

text: Golden banners of “People's Capitalism,” unfurled by G. Keith Funston, once waved above the New York Stock Exchange, and there was a time when Merrill Lynch was bearish on America. Now the standards of “People’s Capitalism,” tattered by the blasts of market declines and the recession, have been struck, but Merrill Lynch is assertedly bullish—at least for the long term.</br></br>Robert Sobel recalls these vagaries of the stock market as well as the main currents of change over the past 40 years—"its most turbulent era.” He recounts the crises that have been encountered and the adjustments that have been made at the Exchange during the period. "N.Y.S.E.” is a detailed, unofficial history of the Exchange, but the Hofstra University professor has in all honesty modulated the impor- tance of his subject. As he notes in his preface: “Once it might have been argued that Wall Street was the power center of the land, but that period ended with the advent of the New Deal and the Great Depression. Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, not Wall Street in New York, is the proper symbol for America in its imperial age.” He adds: “This in not to say that the N.Y.S.E. was unimportant, but rather that its significance in the scheme of things is often misunderstood and exaggerated.”</br></br>The Exchange has been shcm of much of its power. The Securities and Exchange Commission, created during the New Deal, has restricted the market’s operations with successive regulations, the most recent of which stripped the Big Board of its fixed commission rates and established a “consolidated tape.” The new tape reports trading in the Exchange’s stocks along with that at other exchanges throughout the country.</br></br>Although the regulations have further reduced the Exchange’s strength, they do not remove the necessity for a continuing central “auction" market for securities. This basic need for a main shop at which stocks may be traded with some degree of confidence, and prices established, insures that the N.Y.S.E., or something like it, will endure so long as the economic system retains freedom for the individual to own and to buy and sell property.</br></br>Not that, as Professor Sobel points out, reforms were not needed. The individual investor wanted assurance that stocks were not blatantly misrepresented, that he could buy and sell shares at a fair market price, that his funds and his stocks were reasonably safe with a broker, and that manipulators would not have a completely free hand to do in the shareholder. Some salients remain to be tidied up before the individual investor, now bearing scars from one generation to the next, will not flinch at the sound of a low quotation.

text: Like radiation, inflation charges the air around us with invisible menace. Soon, there may be an official statistic: inflation deaths. People will simply keel over at the counter, felled by the high cost of living. Even those who can afford to Dav mav not be able to withstand the stress of rapidly rising prices. Watching the economic indicators can endanger our health. Blood pressure can link up to the prime, and hypertensive types may just slump over and die, their deaths attributed to “the silent killer.”</br></br>Not everyone will die of inflation, but most of us will feel sick. Hyperinflation can lead to hyperventilation, causing people to pant and gasp on what used to be routine shopping expeditions.</br></br>If inflation doesn’t make you physically ill, it will certainly make you a little crazy. Economic stress causes several mental illnesses. The most common: “low-grade-double-digit depression.” The symptoms are subtle, resembling radiation disease: nausea, hair loss, overall numbness and loss of purpose. That syndrome of “Yes, the birds are chirping but I don’t care — my rent is $1,300 and I just paid $2.39 for a little box of blueberries and they weren’t even that wonderful,” There is no known cure. Most victims of low-grade-double-digit depression simply lie around, thinking thoughts like, “The consumer price index is up again, I can’t go on.” They live quietly in unstabilized apartments, feeling their savings ebb. When they go to the bank, they experience the agony of withdrawal, which can bring on a crisis in the condition.</br></br>During a crisis, the deeply depressed person may suffer the classic sleep disturbance — he bolts upright in bed at 3 A.M., staring into the blackness with alarmed eyes, his brain a calculator of pain: “I have not paid the minimum on my Visa charge. I’m being penalized at the rate of 18 percent and I don’t know how their timetable works.” These thoughts, sind worse, will rush, in a torrent of senseless mathematical computations, through the victim’s cerebral cortex until he at last falls into a light and tormented rest. Experts insist the crisis will subside, that the condition itself is “self-limiting."</br></br>The second most prevalent form of inflation sickness is “over-financed schizophrenia.” Onset generally occurs in young adults in the 30- to 42-year-old range. The first symptoms often appear after a major investment. The classic case history: Couple buys a $350,000 co-op, then scrimps on floor wax. Victims exhibit “inappropriate” behavior: They install high-priced carpeting, then fall to the floor clawing at a used vacuum cleaner bag, extracting plumes of lint, rather than invest 57 cents in a new paper vacuum sack.

The upswing has been fueled mainly by heavy institutional buying.</br></br>Many analysts contend that the stock market’s consolidation likely will end soon after Labor Day if only because of the need for the cash-rich institutions to enter the market again in force.</br></br>Wall Street took in stride unfavorable economic news last week. This included an increase in the prime rate by many of the nation’s banks to a record 12>/4 percent from 12 percent.</br></br>Another depressant was the Government’s report that the July index of leading economic indicators fell four-tenths of 1 percent. It was the third decline in the index in four months and indicated a deepening economic slowdown.
metadata__headline: THE MARKETS Consolidating Summer's Gains

text: One prospect is certain for air fares: Like much else in this time of inflation, they are going up, up, up.</br></br>Much of the airline advertising implies otherwise. Bargain fares continue to proliferate on some routes. Also, as summer nears its end and vacation travel ebbs, fares traditionally dip from those of peak season.</br></br>Nonetheless, a comparison of rates announced for this fall with those of a year ago shows across-the-board increases are conspicious on most routes. The principal reason: the soaring cost of jet fuel. Because of continuing uncertainty over fuel availability and cost, fares could rise again and again on relatively short notice.</br></br>The main resistance to rising fares is airline competition. The more competitive a route, the greater the chance of finding a bargain. But bargain fares are rising, too, although there are a few notable exceptions, such as the $108 one-way coach fare between New York and California. Officials of the major coast-to-coast airlines make it clear, however, that they would readily abandon that fare if only it would be dropped by the comparatively small World Airways, which initiated it.</br></br>All this creates special burdens for the traveler. So many fare changes are taking place so fast that it is extremely difficult for even airline professionals to keep abreast.
metadata__headline: Keeping Abreast of the Air Fares: Practical Traveler

text: The most closely watched barometer of the stock market — the Dow Jones industrial average —. forged ahead last week, posting a gain of 6.40 points to finish at 846.16. Its closing high for this year stands at 878.72 on April 10.</br></br>Meanwhile, other market indicators performed rather handsomely. The composite index of all equities listed on the New York Stock Exchange chalked up its best reading of the year. The American Stock Exchange’s market value index came within striking distance of its record high and the NASDAQ composite index, which tracks the progress of over-the-counter stocks, moved to the loftiest level since its introduction in 1971.</br></br>It was, in short, a rather good week for the stock market, despite all the lingering worries about inflation, energy, future unemployment rates and recession.</br></br>In the fixed-income sector, the Treasury’s August financing was well received and bond prices produced a brisk rally.</br></br>While many stock market investors were looking over their shoulders at the Dow, Arnold Bernhard kept his sights on the future. He is the owner of a financial services company best known for its Value Line Investment Survey, the world’s largest investment advisory service.
metadata__headline: Article 4 -- No Title: THE MARKETS A Good Week for the Dow

text: Major American publishing houses are encouraging more outside packagers to produce books for them and are employing more freelance editorial workers than ever before. They are doing so because inflation has raised the cost of producing books while buyers are counting their dollars more carefully before purchasing the latest novel tne moment it comes out. Publishers find it financially advantageous to keep the number of permanent staff members down and to use outsiders; at the same time, these outsiders offer creative innovations.</br></br>Packagers are independents who produce books off the premises for the name publishing houses. Sometimes the packagers initiate book projects and sometimes they work in conjunction with in-house editors. They range from one-man operations to fairly large shops that include freelance writers, editors, designers and artists. 300 Companies Listed</br></br>Nearly 300 companies are listed under “consulting and editorial services” in Literary Market Place, the standard book directory. They describe themselves as capable of delivering “complete editorial and production services, writing projects, book and jacket design, educational, trade, fiction.”</br></br>One individual widely recognized as a pioneer in mass-market paperback and large-size trade paperback packaging is Ian Ballantine, who was president of Bantam Books, later established Ballantine Books and has been in the book field for 40 years.</br></br>Mr. Ballantine, known for his marketing instincts, played a part in the phenomenally successful “Gnomes” package, a Harry N. Abrams hardcover book in which Bantam invested and obtained paperback rights. Mr. Ballantin was also involved in two Abrams followups, “Faeries” and “Giants.” Both were designed by David Larkin, a British bookman who works with Mr. Ballantine.
metadata__headline: Publishers Turning to Packagers and Freelances to Reduce Expenses: 300 Companies Listed 20 Writers and Editors

text: As if to underline the findings of a Presidential advisory panel that inflation “batters” the poof, just after the Department of Labor reported on Thursday that the Consumer Price Index showed an inflation rate of 13.2 percent over the first six months of this year, ... news came over the wires uroan from San Antonio that 91-</br></br>The annual report of the National Advisory Council on Economic Opportunity, made public last Monday, said that “the households in the lowest 10 percent of income distribution spend more than 119 percent of after-tax income" on necessities. The council’s analysis was based on a finding that the current inflationary surge was led by food, energy, housing and medical costs. text: The long-anticipated recession was officially declared weeks ago, but last week the economic indicators were still catching up.</br></br>In July, it turns out, retail sales actually edged up four-tenths of 1 percent. But that report, like most others, was riddled with abberations. The gain, in this case, it didn’t take account of the inflation rate, which exceeded 1 percent for July.</br></br>Then there was the news that food prices dropped 17 percent in the last three months. Indeed they have, at the wholesale level. But at the supermarkets, the price continued to rise — arousing warnings from President Carter that retailers should re-examine their pricing policies. He cited an “extraordinary” increase in the spread between farm and store prices —109 percent for meat, for example.</br></br>So it was with personal income. It took a whopping $27.2 billion jump last month, the largest gain this year and probably greater than the income lost to inflation. But the only real beneficiaries were retirees. They received hefty cost-of-living increases in their Social Security and veterans’ pension payments. For everyone else, purchasing power continued to slip.</br></br>To the Federal Reserve — and its new chairman, Paul A. Volcker — the real problem remains inflation, which it sees as a serious threat to the future of the dollar and the stability of trade and oil prices. Taking a major political gamble that tighter money will both strengthen foreign confidence and slow runaway domestic inflation, it raised the discount rate — the interest on loans to its member banks — to a record 10V£ percent. The step followed by a day action to push up the overnight rate on interbank loans, a move that sent the prime rate at commercial banks soaring to 12 percent, equaled only in 1974. Meanwhile, the money supply, posting its second large increase in a row, expanded by $1 billion in the latest week.
metadata__headline: The Economy: Thunder and Lightning, But Little Rain

text: PRESIDENT CARTER and his top advisers feel that the Presidnt had "absolutely no choice,” as Ambassador Robert S. Strauss put it, but to nominate a tough and independent monetary conservative like Paul A. Volcker as chairman of the Federal Reserve Board.</br></br>But they recognize that, if the economy goes into an even deeper recession than they currently are expecting, the Administration’s economic policy could face a cruel dilemma — and the President could face a grave political problem — over whether to stick with a restrictive monetary policy with unemployment mounting in an election year.</br></br>Nevertheless, the White House went with Mr. Volcker to reassure the markets that the dollar was not headed for a still-worse nosedive. In the view of Mr. Carter’s advisers, the dollar has become a critical measure of the American economy’s performance— and a determinant of how not just foreigners but the American people themselves feel about their country. In the short run, Mr. Volcker has unquestionably been worth some huge multiple of his weight in gold, even at more than $300 an ounce.</br></br>There was general recognition at the top of the Carter Administration that, in the midst of the developing dollar crisis, monetary policy would be more con- strained for the immediate future than under normal circumstances, no matter who was chairman of the Fed—Mr. Volcker, his predecessor; G. William Miller, who is the newly designated Secretary of the Treasury, or anyone else.</br></br>"In the context of a renewed attack on the dollar,” Stuart E. Eizenstat, the President’s assistant for doomestic affairs and policy, said in an interview, “if we hadntt moved boldly, the nation would never have got to the long-term dilemma, no matter who the new Federal Reserve chairman was.”
metadata__headline: Economic Scene: Money Policy: Hard Choices

text: THROUGHOUT his long career as an economic adviser, John Maynard Keynes sought to demonstrate that the government, faced with an economic crisis, need not stand by helplessly. A correct analysis of the problem, he believed, would always suggest some effective course of action the government could take.</br></br>Today the crisis is one of double-digit inflation rather than double-digit unemployment. But as in Keynes's day the government seems unable to do anything about it. And the reason, again, is that the majority of economists are unable to provide a correct analysis of the problem.</br></br>The consensus among economists is that inflation stems from excess demand, and for this reason they urge policies to curtail the expansion of the economy. However, there is little evidence to support either the diagnosis or the prescription.</br></br>It is against this background that a small but growing minority of economists have offered a different explanation for inflation. The continual rise in prices, these post-Keynesians argue, stems from conflicts over the distribution of a growing social surplus.</br></br>Post-Keynesians emphasize that the distributional issues can be seen in three dynamic processes that, in conjunction with one another, have led to the unprecedented inflation of the past decade. The three processes and associated conflicts are: 9A domestic wage-price spiral, with labor struggling with capital for a larger share of the internally produced social surplus.
metadata__headline: Economic Scene: New Approach On Inflation

text: WASHINGTON, Aug. 7—The Carter Administration acknowledged today that the recent unexpected surge in inflation had created problems in extending its wage-price guidelines for a second year but predicted the oncom ing recession would make the program work better by checking both wage and price increases.</br></br>Alfred E. Kahn, chairman of the Council on Wage aiid Price Stability, told reporters in announcing proposals for new standards in the second year that slack markets were already developing in raw materials, a development that would help in the enforcement of new price standards.</br></br>He also said that the recession would make the threat of debarment from Government contracts a more powerful weapon against noncomplying com panies, but he declined to outline what the Government’s reaction would be if new auto-industry wage settlements violated the guidelines.</br></br>“It will make our life tougher," said Mr. Kahn, later quipping, “I didn’t create the world; I nave to live in it. ”</br></br>The United Automobile Workers union has already served notice that it will not be bound by any Government pay standards in bargaining with the auto industry.

text: WASHINGTON, July 10 — President Carter has decided against removing controls from the cost of gasoline because he believes that prices would rise more sharply than they already have and worsen inflation, his press secretary, Jody Powell, announced today.</br></br>However, White House aides expect the President to adopt a program intended to reduce oil imports by four million to five million barrels a day next year through conservation and the use of synthetic fuels and alternative energy sources.</br></br>Decontrol of gasoline prices has been a hotly contested subject within the Administration. Secretary of Energy James R. Schlesinger has argued that decontrol would be the boldest stoke available for dealing with the immediate gasoline shortage. Other officials, however, have argued against it, fearing an angry response from consumers.</br></br>Aides worked into the night to prepare a memorandum setting forth specific options to deliver tomorrow morning to the President at Camp David.</br></br>The Carter stand on a phased decontrol of domestic crude oil prices with a tax on "windfall” oil-company profits was endorsed today by the National Governors Association, but it also backed tax relief for companies’ “plowing back” profits into new energy development, which is opposed by the Administration. text: President Carter nominated Paul A. Volcker, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and a leading figure in international financial circles, to be chairman of the Federal Reserve Board yesterday.</br></br>At a news conference after his nomination, Mr. Volcker said he was committed to fighting inflation and restoring international confidence in the dollar and the American econony. “Inflation certainly is the priority,” he said.</br></br>A primary goal would be to create a “sense of restoration of stability,” he said, adding that the nation could not achieve it without the “fact of stability.” Business and banking leaders, both in this country and Europe, reacted enthusiastically to the nomination. text: WASHINGTON, Aug. 12 — The average American is likely to see his standard of living drastically reduced in the 1980’s unless productivity growth is accelerated, the Joint Economic Committee, a Congressional body, wamedtoday.</br></br>In its midyear analysis of economic prospects, the committee said that a dismal future could be avoided only if the Government acted now to raise the economy’s productive potential. It described productivity growth, or greater output per man-hour, as the “economic linchpin of thel980’s."</br></br>The committee, the economic conscience of Congress, is influential in that most of its members head or sit on other powerful committees, such as banking, finance or ways and means. It is charged with guiding Congressional committees that deal with economic matters.</br></br>Fundamental weaknesses in the economy would emerge even in the absence of oil-price problems, the report stated, because growth in productivity is lagging behind growth rates in all the major trading nations.</br></br>In the first half this year, output per man-hour in the total private business sector decreased by an annual rate of 3.3 percent, while productivity in the nonfarm private business sector fell at an annual rate of 5.7 percent, the largest quarterly decline ever recorded in this series of statistics, which began in 1947. The nation’s productivity did increase, however, by 5.3 percent in 1977 and by 4.4 percent lastyear.

text: PARIS, July 25 — European monetary officials and bankers welcomed today’s nomination of Paul A. Volcker, president of the New York Federal Reserve Bank, to be chairman of the Federal Reserve Board, and the battered dollar moved slightly Higher.</br></br>But they cautioned that Mr. Volcker, despitehis proven record in private banking, at the United States Treasury and in the central bank, might face some bruising battles. In attempting to restore confidence in the dollar, as both he and President Carter today said they wanted to do, he will have to contend with an electionconscious Administration and Congress, the officials and bankers warned.</br></br>in Bonn, West Germany’s Finance Minister, Hans Matthofer, described the choice of Mr. Volcker as “extraordinarily good” and added, “I am sure he will continue to represent the policies of stabilization.'’</br></br>In Frankfurt, Otmar Emminger, president of the Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, said: “Paul Volcker is very well known in all international financial circles and enjoys their full confidence. I personally have had many years of very close'cooperation with him, and I am confident that Mr. Volcker’s nomination will contribute to a strengthening of confidence in the dollar. ” “This is excellent news,” commented Hans Bar, a partner in the big Zurich Bank of Julius Bar. “Paul Volcker is a disciplinarian with a sense of international responsibility.” Other European bankers also felt that the Reserve Board would be in safe hands with Mr.^olcker. They cited his knowledge of international finance and his understanding and respect for the dollar’s pivotal role in the international monetary system.</br></br>- In London, Peter Wing of Morgan Grenfell, a merchant bank, observed that Mr. Volcker "must be going in on his own terms.” He was referring to the substantial pay cut that Mr. Volcker would take in moving from the New York bank, which pays commercial salaries, to the Federal Reserve Board, where salaries are linked to the lower Federal pay scale. Mr. Volcker’s nomination has thus removed some of the doubts about President Carter’s commitment to fighting inflation and preserving a sound dollar that were raised by last week’s Cabinet shuffle. The abrupt decision to replace the Treasury Secretary, W. Michael Blumenthal, with the current Reserve Board chairman, G. William Miller, had stirred concern among European bankers, who suspect Mr. Miller of political ambitions that might lead him to inflationary policies.

text: WASHINGTON, July 2—The Supreme Court removed a major threat to President Carter’s anti-inflation program today by declining to accept a case testing the program’s constitutionality.</br></br>The Court decided, 6 to 3, hot to hear an appeal by the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations, which had challenged the President’s authority to use the Government’s purchasing power to enforce wage and price guidelines.</br></br>The decision means that the Administration can deny Federal contracts to companies that violate the wage or price guidelines.</br></br>However, a Defense Department spokesman said in an interview today j that the Pentagon had decided to give a I$77 million contract for jet fuel to the Amerada Hess Corporation, one of only two companies that the Government has listed so far as having violated the guidelines.</br></br>The large oil refining and marketing company had previously said that "we regret’’ that the price guidelines, as established by the Government, “do not allow Amerada Hess to comply.’’

text: THE basic inflation rate, measured by the growth of industrial prices, is now more than 10 percent. With the recently announced price rise by the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, this rate will soon go even higher, with no pros-neet of its diminishine in the near future.</br></br>As painful as So rapid a decline in the purchasing power of money may be, the seeming inability of the Government to do anything about it is perhaps even more disheartening.</br></br>The apparent helplessness of the Government in the face of inflation seems all the more puzzling when one realizes that the Carter Administration, like its predecessors, has generally followed the prescription of “mainstream” economists in its efforts to combat the steep rise hi prices. Only when one examines the prescription itself, and the explanation for inflation from which it derives, does the helplessness of the Government become less puzzling.</br></br>Most economists maintain—the exceptions will be noted shortly—that inflation stems from “excess demand.” The disagreement is largely over whether the excess demand arises from the actions of the Federal Reserve Board in allowing the money supply to increase too rapidly (“too much money chasing too few goods”) or from the actions of Congress in voting to spend more funds than can be raised from taxes ("the evil of Government deficits”).</br></br>Thus, the advice that an Administration receives from its economic advisers invariably involves putting a brake on economic expansion. And since the ability to fine-tune the economy is limited, especially on the downside, this inevitably means a deliberately induced recession.
metadata__headline: Economic Scene: New Inflation Explanation

text: A consensus has developed among private economists that the United States economy is entering a recession, although most of them agree that it will be nowhere nearly as severe as in 1974 and 1975.</br></br>That expectation, which gained a most distinguished adherent yesterday when President Carter said he considered a recession “much more likely” following the latest oil price increase by the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, came to light in both a report by a private research group and in interviews with other economists.</br></br>The Economic Forum of the Conference Board, a group of economists and business analysts that released its semi-annual report on the economy yesterday, predicted a mild recession during the last half of 1979, to be followed by a gradual recovery in 1980.</br></br>Seven of the 12 economists participating in the Forum forecast two or more quarters of negative real economic growth — the definition of a recession.</br></br>And, noted Albert T. Sommers, chief economist at the Conference Board, if the group had met after the oil cartel’s price increases were set, rather than on June 7, “the expectations would probably have been somewhat more somber.”

text: GLADWYNE, Pa. — While cutting my hair, my barber explained that “big business is creating inflation to increase profits.” Since I was eager to improve my company’s profit, I pressed for more details of how I could make inflation work for me. As my barber-economist went on, his explanation developed that well-known Washington fuzziness.</br></br>“Listen,” he said, “big business runs the country, right? We’ve got more inflation than ever, right? Who causes it if it isn’t big business and why would they do it if it wasn’t to increase their profit?” Now eager to end the ordeal, I weakly muttered, “Guess you’re right,” and went back to my newspaper.</br></br>Driving home that evening, I was angry because I hadn’t even tried to clear up one more muddled mind. Too many Americans believe that my barber made good sense and that more Government regulation of business would make things right with the world again.</br></br>I should have told my barber that price increases are not inflation but are the result of inflation. I should have told him that inflation is really caused by our Government when it prints too much paper money, much of which is needed to support a nonproductive bureaucracy that regulates and controls our lives. Since prices inevitably rise when an excess of purchasing media is created, our Government then tries to minimize price increases through controls and bv shift- ing the blame onto business. Price controls follow, followed, in turn, by export controls in a futile attempt to shore up a sagging economic system. The price control on domestic crude oil is one example of the never-ending litany of controls that isn’t working because the incentive for domestic oil exploration and production has been diminished.</br></br>Steel shortages are already developing as steel migrates to foreign markets that will pay higher prices. Soon we will have export controls to protect us against steel shortages. Too few of us realize that the Treasury printing presses are the real engines of inflation fueling a spending spree fostered by those elected to lead but who have failed to do so. Politicians will consider this explanation simplistic, but I consider it a return to the fundamentals of a sound economic system.

text: WASHINGTON, July 16 (AP) — The number of working Americans declined slightly during the second quarter of 1979, the.first dip in employment since the 1974-75 recession, the Labor Department reported today.</br></br>The report was in line with the Carter Administration’s predictions that unemployment would rise this year arid next as the economy heads into a mild recession'..</br></br>The Labor Department said employment totaled 96.4 million people during the April-June quarter, down from 96.6 million during the first three months of the year.</br></br>The last time employment fell was in the first quarter of 1975, when the number of working Americans dropped to 84.4 million from 85.6 million in the last quarter of 1974.</br></br>The percentage of Americans who are 16 or older and hold jobs also declined slightly during the second quarter, to 59.1 percent, compared to a record 59.4 percent during the first quarter.

text: WASHINGTON — In the cold glare of hindsight, the world’s adjustment to the 1973-74 Arab oil embargo and the consequent quadrupling of crude oil prices served principally to buy time, five years of it. Now the piper has returned to be paid again. The question is how, and principally whether, this time long-term policies to provide a smoother adjustment to new energy realities will be put in place. As Theodore Eck, chief economist at the Standard Oil Company (Indiana), puts it: “If we balance out because of a recession, the politicians are going to go back to sleep. It would be the right answer for the wrong reason.” --Balance out" may De a bit arcane. But Mr. Eck’s prediction is quite simple and to most energy experts, quite worrisome. As in 1973-55, market forces will chew away at the United States’ energy difficulties, and, barring new political problems in the oil-producing countries, what Secretary of Energy James R. Schlesinger last week called “a fragile balance” will probably be reached by year-end.</br></br>It will, however, be a balance achieved principally through the effects of higher oil prices—possibly 50 percent higher than they were at the end of 1978. Gasoline will likely average more than 90 cents a gallon; more volatile home heating oil is almost certain to rise as quickly. Even those estimates could prove low if world oil prices spurt again, beyond the catch-up increase expected from Saudi Arabia.</br></br>The inevitable consumer reaction is to search for ways to reduce energy consumption. Already, they are flocking to smaller cars, or in some cases, to no cars at all, as the 20.2 percent slide in car sales in the last week week in May suggest. Home insulation, more efficient Industrial processes and fuel-saving planes will all receive a further boost.</br></br>All told, says John Lichtblau, executive director of the Petroleum Industry Research Foundation, next year may well be marked by no increase in oil use, just as, although in a more dramatic way, oil use fell after the much larger 1973-74 price increases. Meanwhile, the supply curve will receive a boost. Higher international prices for oil spur domestic exploration; President Carter’s recent decontrol program would allow American producers to receive them as well.</br></br>which strain the American patience and well-being, possibly into recession, are another repetition of effects that policy makers had hoped needed not be borne. Failing to avoid them holds now great political consequences for President Carter. His predecessor, President Ford, presided over a similar adjustment process and was not re-elected. According to projections by Data Resources Inc., a well-known consulting firm, by 1980, the rise in oil prices could reduce growth by a substantial one percentage point, and raise the inflation rate by one point as well.

text: To understand what that means, an investor must know what a yield curve is, how one is plotted and what its uses are. With that understanding, he’ll have a useful tool to help him increase his total return from fixed-income investments. He will also know what the investment community as a whole believes to be the outlook for interest rates — though there is no assurance that this consensus will prove to be correct.</br></br>Joseph Bench, money market economist at First Pennco Securities, a leading Government securities firm, recently charted a yield curve for United States Treasury securities. When he had completed his work, he concluded that “interest rates are expected to be lower next year than they are today.” To the uninitiated, Mr. Bench’s yield curve, drawn in a clear, bold line, looked a little like a headline in an Arab newspaper.</br></br>The Morgan Guaranty Trust Company’s Money-Market Letter plots yield curves each week, and it has reached much the same conclusion. Yield curves since last summer, Morgan’s letter said recently, suggest “a peaking and downdrift in short rates.”</br></br>A yield curve is simply a diagram that illustrates the relationship between rates of return and maturities of similar fixed-income securities. Frequently, Treasury bills, notes and bonds are used for this exercise because they provide a complete range of maturities for securities that all carry the same degree of risk. To draw a yield curve, set out the maturities on graph paper on a horizontal line from left to right starting with the nearest and continuing out to the most distant. Then plot the yields for each maturity on the vertical axis, connecting the dots with a line that becomes the yield curve. At different times, these graphs look very different, and they are informative.</br></br>As Mr. Bench put it: “Money and capital market relationships of yield and term to maturity tell us the market’s expectations of future interest rate trends.” prove to be accurate forecasts of future interest rate trends, there are wide variations in the time lapses before the changes come true. text: WASHINGTON — A jarring equation is gaining credence among the senior officials of the Carter Administration: Lack of progress in the fight against inflation equals a Republican President in 1980. And the consumer price index averaged a 13 percent annualized increase for the first two months. That, as compared with a consumer price index of 9 percent in 1978 and 7 percent in 1977.</br></br>Quietly, without public announcement or even broad circulation within official channnels, the Troika, as it is known — the Office of Management and Budget, Council on Economic Advisers and the Treasury Department — was recently forced to revise their official inflation forecast of 7.5 percent for 1979. It is believed that the new projection is about 1 percentage point higher than the previous official estimate, but many of the President’s advisers believe that even the new projection is too optimistic.</br></br>The Administration decided last week against announcing its new inflation forecast in part because officials did not wish to throw yet another obstacle in the path of their political program. The Teamsters union, however, id not need the Administration’s new official forecast to divine that a 7 percent annual increase in members’ pay would not keep pace with future inflation. The collapse of the negotiating effort was nevertheless a setback in the Administration’s jaw-boning campaign.</br></br>Most White House watchers agreed long ago that real wage insurance, once portrayed as the lynchpin of President Carter’s voluntary anti-inflation program, stood no chance of winning Congressional approval. text: The economic recovery turned 4 years old this month, making it one of the longest business expansions on :ecord. But economists who follow business cycles say the unusual length of the current growth phase does not by itself mean that a downturn is near.</br></br>"It isn’t the age of a cycle per se that makes a difference,” says F. Thomas Juster, director of the Institute for Social Research at the University of Michigan. "It’s a question of going for a certain amount of time and finding that things get out of balance.”</br></br>To Mr. Juster and many other business cycle economists, signs of imbalances that might signal a recession simply have not appeared. If they are right, that could mean good news for the Carter Administration but bad news for those who believe a recession is necessary to bring down the level of inflation. However this outlook puts them at odds with many other economists who have already forecast the peaking of the current economic expansion and who say that a recession will hit sometime later this year.</br></br>“There’s been too much talk about a recession coming when that’s not clear at all,” says Solomon Fabricant, a staff member emeritus and director of the National Bureau of Economic Research, the long-standing arbiter of what is a recession and what is not.</br></br>The business cycle, which underlies their analysis and predictions, serves as a yardstick for comparing current economic activity with previous periods. The cycle is nothing more than a four-part pattern: a period of economic growth, a peak in that growth, a period of slower growth or actual decline in the economy and a trough — after which growth starts anew. Since the 1850’s, there have been 23 peacetime expansions with an average duration of 26 months.

text: President Carter would now be facing a first-class dilemma over oil and inflation even if nothing had happened in Iran. Rarely do competing Interests involve such a head-on collision: • Mr. Carter should be doing everytmng ne can to restrain the nation’s appetite for imported oil. Cour- . tesy of a 1975 law, he has at his fingertips a highly effective way to do that: lift the existing price controls. When oil costs more, people use less.</br></br>• Mr. Carter should be doing everything he can to restrain inflation,( the more so given Friday’s grim news that consumer prices are rising at double-digit annual rates. And he has at his fingertips an effective way to do that — by refusing to lift price controls on oil. Higher prices could vitiate other Administration efforts to combat inflation.</br></br>There is no easy way out of the dilemma, which is why we have in the past recommended the course that 'is generally advisable when irresistible force meets immovable object: split the difference, deregulate oil prices gradually. America must pay for oil; Iran shows there can be a higher price than money.</br></br>Full deregulation of oil prices now might add 6 cents a gallon to the price of gas at the pump. text: HOW severe will this recession be? How long will it last, and which sectors of the economy will be hit the hardest? Any effort to answer those questions depends first on grasping the special character of this recession.</br></br>Every recession, as the late Wesley C. Mitchell of Columbia used to stress, is unique. The 1948-49 recession was essentially an inventory recession, for instance, brought on by the cessation of postwar stockpiling. The 1953-54 recession resulted mainly from the heavy cutback of Federal spending after the Korean War. The 1957-58 recession was caused by the overshooting of a capital spending boom — but that recession was first delayed by a burst of Government spending related to the Suez crisis and then intensified by defense order cutbacks and Federal Reserve monetary tightening.</br></br>If it had not been for consumers cutting their savings rate down to a historic low of 3 percent and going so deeply into debt, the expansion would not have lasted as long as it did; the recession would probably have begun in the final quarter of 1978.</br></br>The current recession is a rarity: a consumer-led recession. As Lawrence Chimerine, president of Chase Econometrics, put it, "Unlike most other recessions, the current downturn is not due to a major weakening in the enterprise sector, or to a postwar decline in military spending. Rather, it is due to the significant weakening in the financial position of households, and the resulting decline in spending for goods, services and homes. ”</br></br>The consumer recession has resulted from the decline in employees’ real income as inflation accelerated, the decline in employment, the record buildup of consumer debt, and the fall in value of household assets, including stocks, bonds, houses and many consumer durables. On top of this, Mr. Chimerine added, "Households are already saving a record low portion of their incomes and are finding it difficult or too expensive to increase borrowing. Thus, there is nothing left to sustain spending. ”

text: THIS fall’s election seems unlikely to alter the consensus that has emerged among the nation’s political leaders and their economic advisers that the necessary cure for inflation is a deliberately induced recession. What is not sufficiently appreciated is the effect that such a cure has on the American economy’s long-run growth rate — not to mention the people who immediately lose their jobs.</br></br>President Carter already stands apart from other recent Democratic chief executives in his open espousal of the recession cure. He has just finished applying this cure to the economy and, while the basic inflation rate has yet to fall, he is quick to point to his policy of restraining growth in the economy whenever one of the price indexes rises by less than in the previous month.</br></br>The President has now promised that, if re-elected, he will move to strengthen his wage-price stabilization program and, indeed, has even won some business and labor support for that effort. But when this and other measures fail to lower the inflation rate, Mr. Carter can be expected to bow to advice that he apply further restraint on the economy.</br></br>Ronald Reagan might at first appear to offer an alternative set of policies. Certainly his proposal that Federal taxes be reduced by 30 percent over three years while expenditures are cut back by only 10 percent stands in sharp contrast to President Carter’s insistence on a balanced budget. Still, whatever might be the effect of these policies on the long-term growth rate — and there is no reason to believe that the effect would not be a positive one — they hardly speak to the inflation issue.</br></br>In fact, when one passes from Mr. Reagan’s campaign statements to his list of economic advisers, it becomes clear what his anti-inflationary policy is likely to be. The advisers are many of the same group who persuaded previous Republican Presidents to apply the recession cure and thereby produce the economic downturns of 1953, 1958, 1960 and 1974. (The 1969 downturn was largely the respon- sibility of the preceding Democratic Administration.) If the anti-inflationary policy of a Reagan Administration is to differ from that of Mr. Carter, it will merely be that, in the words of the Reagan advisers, the recession cure will be applied “more quickly” and allowed to continue longer.

text: INFLATION. For years it crept along silently like a cat, barely noticed. Then it changed shape and grew bolder, but remained more or less friendly. In the United States, where high discretionary incomes and an immense choice of goods limited its impact, it seemed that only foreigners had seen inflation’s really savage side.</br></br>Now the beast is easily visible, a luminescent specter, a killer, a threat to society, public enemy No. 1.</br></br>How did this monster get loose? What and who does it feed on? How can it be tamed? Just what is inflation, anyway, this rapacious thing that devours paychecks, savings and peace of mind?</br></br>A surge in the price of wheat, Manhattan office space, mortgage money, scalped tickets to the Super Bowl, houses in Washington, oil or small cars may indeed raise the cost of living. But individually they don’t constitute inflation. They can result from crop failure, business-cycle shortage, anti-inflation measures, a ’’Cinderella’’ football team, zoning requirements, a foreign cartel, revolution or simply a change in consumer preferences.</br></br>That is what the United States has. In 1979, the Consumer Price Index went up 13.3 percent, the highest one-year rate since 1946. More important, while price increases were less than 2 percent a year for much of the 1950’s and 1960’s they started the 1970’s at 5.2 percent, and have escalated steadily for the past four years.

text: THE odds dictated by election-year politics and recession-year economics favor a tax cut in 1980, but President Carter, who has been advised to keep his options open as long as possible, may make no final decisions until well into the first quarter.</br></br>With 1979 producing a set of confounding economic statistics — an unexpectedly buoyant economy depressed unemployment while inflation ran red-hot — the President was urged to defer tax proposals at least until a few of the 1980 numbers are wrung from the statistical mills. text: WASHINGTON — To brace the public for bad news and prepare the way for possible antirecession actions, Ray Marshall, President Carter’s Secretary of Labor, last week warned that the unemployment rate could climb above 6.5 percent by midyear and still higher by year-end.</br></br>But there was no sign of such deterioration in figures for December released by the Labor Department Friday. Some analysts thought they saw early signs in a decline in the ratio of black teenagers with jobs, to 26.2 percent In December from 28 percent early in 1979. ,</br></br>Mr. Marshall’s forecast was interesting in two ways. It could be considered optimistic. text: WASHINGTON — It has become a byword among economists that the Government invariably intervenes too late to save the economy from the ravages of a recession, and that the principal effect of antirecessionary measures is to aggravate inflation when the business cycle starts its next UDswine.</br></br>Liberals usually say the lid should have been lifted on anti-inflation policies sooner. Conservatives generally argue that the country would have been better off and inflation ameliorated if Washington had let economy's natural regenerative forces do their work.</br></br>Both sides are dusting off their arguments. With unemployment moving up (to 7 percent in April) and inflation coming down (the smallest wholesale price increase in 11 months was reported last week), some Administration officials have already begun to sketch possible antirecession measures.</br></br>In the Labor Department, there is talk of more Federally funded local-government jobs. The Budget Office is braced to resist an expected push from the construction trades, the Congressional Black Caucus and the nation’s mayors for a fresh round of local public works spending. Some White House officials even wonder whether President Carter could endorse tax reduction in time for passage in 1980, and not be accused again of bending with the breeze.</br></br>It is all a reminder that despite the sophisticated theories of Keynesian fiscal policy and Friedmanite monetary policy, those who practice political economy — economists as well politicians — have yet to show that they can flatten the business cycle.

text: WILL they or won’t they stay longer on the job? Little research has been done on the subject.</br></br>George McCullough, manager of management relations at Exxon, tends to think that potential retirees may begin to rethink early retirement, but the company has no figures so far to support a change in a long-term trend toward early retirement. text: Americans need no additional proof that inflation is a critical concern to everyone, but those who order proof coin sets are getting it just the same — and they’re getting proof of inflation in the form of inflation o! proofs.</br></br>The United States Mint is charging $10 each for its 1980 proof sets. text: WASHINGTON, March 26 — For the first time since they wrongly declared a recession under way last year, senior Administration officials have begun to contend openly that the long-awaited economic slowdown has at last commenced.</br></br>The growing conviction that a recession is probably under way is based on an array of economic statistics that, while not conclusive, provide evidence of substantial and increasing economic weakness.</br></br>“The February data definitely look like a weakening to me,” said Courtenay M. text: THE most serious problem facing economic theorists and policy makers is how to break the cycle of inflationary expansion, credit crunch, recession and stimulative efforts that result in new inflation in which the United States economy is caught.</br></br>There is nothing accidental about this cycle. It has deep historical roots. During Franklin Roosevelt’s first term, the economic role of Government was greatly expanded to rescue the nation from depression. Hopes that the American economy would never again fall into that kind of depression have been strengthened by the economy's ability to bounce back from recessions — even the worst recession of the postwar period, in 1973-75.</br></br>Prof. Hyman P. Minsky of Washington University in St. Louis says that the economy today is facing dangers even greater than those of the mid-1970’s. However, in a forthcoming article in Challenge magazine, he contends that it will weather the storm, because of the changes in the economic system since 1929.</br></br>The most important change, he maintains, is in the way Government debt offsets shortfalls in business profits. In 1929 the slump in business investment was not offset by a climb in Government debt, and the cash available to business to fulfill commitments on debts fell by 23.5 percent. A rise in Government deficit tends to sustain or increase the total demand for joods and services. In 1975, though business investment slumped by $23.7 billion from 1974, the Federal Budget deficit climbed past $70 billion, almost $60 billion higher than in 1974. As a result, Professor Minsky calculates, business gross retained earnings climbed to $176 billion in 1975, more than $38 billion higher than in 1974.</br></br>Thus, during the most serious recession of the postwar period, the cash flow to business after taxes, interest and dividends climbed by 28 percent. However, as Professor Minsky points out, inflation was regenerated to current levels by the ballooning of Government debt.

text: BASEL, Switzerland, June 8 — The Western industrial nations need to strengthen their commitment to fight inflation and cut their dependence on imported oil by preparing to accept a long period of high unemployment, the Bank for International Settlements said in its latest annual report, which was released today.</br></br>For the first time in several years, the bank’s annual survey of the world economy endorses the general direction Western economic policy is now taking. text: Millions of women have entered the labor force in recent years, and a few have worked their way into the upper reaches of the professions and big business. I took $10,000 and put it in the market because that was a dream of mine, to buy and sell on a speculative basis, not as long-term investments. text: In an effort to stimulate sales in the face of high interest rates, some residential developers in the New York metropolitan area have begun to offer buyers a temporary break in the interest rate on their mortgage.</br></br>The effect is to reduce the monthly carrying cost of the house during the early years, in the hope of attracting the “upwardly mobile” buyer in particular.</br></br>The incentive is known in the trade as a “buydown,” and its recent introduction is believed to be the first use of such financing arrangements in the new-construction residential sector in the metropolitan area.</br></br>Generally, the builder pays as much as 2t/2 to 1 percentage points of the interest rate at which the fixed-rate loan closed — about 13 percent under current market conditions — typically for a period of three years. text: BOSTON — The incoming Reagan administration should recognize that its responses to collective bargaining, business-pricing policies, and indexing of various social benefits are elements in the credibility of its anti-inflation efforts. Because developments in these areas are now approaching points of decision, the new administration must act quickly after it takes office Jan. 20.</br></br>Corporate plans for the next five years almost uniformly anticipate inflation running at 10 percent per year. If such compounded rates of price increase continue for the 1980’s, the price level in the United States will more than double by 1990.</br></br>Suggestions of a tax cut are troubling when the Federal budget deficit was $59 billion for the fiscal year just ended, and is expected by some economists to rise in the current fiscal year.</br></br>What is disturbing is not the proposal for a tax cut, which is needed and appropriate, but rather that no answer has been given to the question of how its inflationary impact is to be offset.</br></br>Increased tax revenues stimulated by an expanding economy will provide a partial offset, if they actually occur. But as the Federal deficit increases, the pressure on monetary policy to offset inflationary pressures grows. Financing the Federal deficit this fall has already helped to drive interest rates up dramatically, and now-higher interest rates are cutting into the general economic recovery that was briefly under way. As a result, most economic projections show a sluggish economy next year—one in which economic growth will be constrained by tight monetary policy and in which high interest rates and a large Federal budget deficit will combine to keep inflationary expectations alive.

Secretariat, which monitors the economic health of the 24 member nations, all industrialized, said it expected the United States economy to contract by about five-tenths of</br></br>However, it added today that the downturn would have only a relatively mild impact on American inflation, which the O.E.C.D. expects to exceed 10 percent this year, although it will help end America’s three-year string of big payment deficits by pushing its external accounts lower and into balance with the level of incoming payments.</br></br>If the United States downturn is mild and other major economies experience slow growth — about 1.25 percent this year — the O.E.C.D. suggests, the world will avoid a downturn similar to the one it suffered after the big 1974 oil price rises.</br></br>Although the growth of 1.25 percent would be much slower than in the past and would imply a further rise in unemployment, it is still better than the zero or even negative growth the O.E.C.D. had feared at the start of the year, when oil prices were rising very rapidly.

text: WASHINGTON, Jan. 28 — President Carter sent to Congress today a budget for the fiscal year 1981 that holds the line on most nonmilitary programs, forecasts a mild recession and high unemployment, and omits the usual antirecession, election-year tonic of a tax cut.</br></br>In his Budget Message, Mr. Carter stressed inflation as a long-term problem and asserted that the United States must build up its military strength in a “sometimes hostile world.”</br></br>The President’s spending proposals, subject to Congressional revision, contemplate record outlays of $616 billion, revenues of $600 billion and a deficit of $16 billion in the fiscal year 1981. The year begins next Oct. 1, five weeks before the election in which Mr. Carter hopes to win a second term, and runs through Sept. 30,</br></br>Smaller Deficit Stressed Without referring to his 1976 campaign promise to balance the budget by 1981, Mr. Carter emphasized that the deficit he projected would be the smallest in seven years.</br></br>than are predicted by some private forecasters, and with officials already speculating that Mr. Carter will ask Congress for additional military funds, the prospect that the deficit would be as low as $16 billion seemed slim. Analysts at the Congressional Budget Office said the White House economic projections were only slightly more optimistic than theirs.

text: NOW that the economy is sliding into recession, will the Carter Administration relax its drive for a balanced budget? And will the Federal Reserve relax its restrictive money and credit policies?</br></br>Many businessmen are afraid the Administration may be too rigid, refusing to consider tax cuts until the slump gets out of hand. But the banking and investment communities are more concerned that the fight against inflation will be abandoned too soon, with devastating effects on interest rates and the stock and bond markets.</br></br>How is one to read the news out of Washington? In assuring the auto industry and auto union leaders that help would be forthcoming, was the President sounding retreat along a broad front? In his talk to the National Association of Mutual Savings Banks, in which he said he was looking forward to the end of credit controls, was the Fed chairman, Paul A. Volcker, yielding to pressures from housing, autos and other consumer-oriented industries?</br></br>It appears that both the Administration and the Fed have not altered their fundamental fiscal and monetary policies but have only been maneuvering to contain specific political pressures.</br></br>Secretary of Commerce Philip M. text: In the early days of 1980, inflation hedge stocks were all the rage on Wall Street and investors snapped up companies with assets in the ground — oil, natural gas, precious metals, trees — whatever promised growth equal to or exceeding the Drice SDiral.</br></br>Now, however, recession is the catchword and strategies have turned defensive. With the expectations of shrinking profits and a long dry spell in economic growth, the question is one of survival, or of relative strength in a weak business environment.</br></br>Even rising earnings during a recession won’t necessarily mean a rising price for a given stock, of course. The market collapse of 1973-74 provided a severe object lesson on that score. The rationale, then, is to simply choose the most seaworthy boat around and batten down the hatches for the duration, hoping to make headway in the near future but counting on emerging from the storm in good condition.</br></br>Timing, as always, is a critical element in placing one’s bets, and in some groups of stocks, the best time to jump may already be past.</br></br>“In a sense, we've already witnessed the first wave of opportunity — the purchase of such interest-sensitive issues as electric utilities, telephone companies and regional banks,” noted William G. Garrison, who heads a New York asset management firm bearing his name. “One can make a case that the major gains for these groups already have been made."

text: “THE LOVING PROCESS: WOMEN”—Linda Gray limbers up during a two-part CBS special, part of “The Body Human” series, Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons at 1:30.</br></br>Economics may be the dismal science, but the subject of business is sparkling these days on television. Suddenly, it seems, the home screen is overflowing with talk about “CDs” and Treasury-bill auction rates. The daily report that used to be limited to some brief graphics indicating whether the stock market went up or down has now been expanded to special segments and, in some instances, full half-hours focused on nothing but business news. In addition to the granddaddy of all these shows, “Wall Street Week,” there is “The Nightly Business Report,” also on public television, “Louis Rukeyser’s Business Jounral” onWCBS-TV and “Moneyline” on the Cable News Network. Dow-Jones, publisher of The Wall Street Journal, is supplying short reports to television and radio stations. Elsewhere on cable, there is “This Week on Wall Street,” carried on the Christian Broadcasting Network, and Home Box Office, the pay-cable operation, has launched “Money Matters,” based on Money magazine.</br></br>In a sense, this electronic boom for business only reflects long-developing realities. More people are investing in the stock market. Just 10 years ago, daily volume of 10 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange was considered hefty. Now, 50 million shares is closer to the norm. In addition, the past several years of inflation and oil crises have encouraged many working people to explore sectors of the business market that once were the almost exclusive terrains of the experts and the very wealthy.</br></br>For the most part, though, television has had a difficult time in getting a handle on economics reporting. Government reports and corporate balance sheets are not only complicated but persistently nonvisual in terms of television action. How do you illustrate the gross national product? Reports on inflation have settled into the numbingly repetitive shots of grocery carts being wheeled down the aisles of supermarkets. But television news is gradually realizing that it must go beyond the familiar props to show how economics has profound influences on the everyday lives of ordinary people. There is one problem: Capturing those stories on tape can be an expensive proposition, requiring on-location shooting and well-informed correspondents. Unusual commitment is required. ABC, for instance, has been frequently impressive with some of the multipart reports by Dan Cordtz on the “Evening News.”</br></br>The more specialized formats still rely heavily on the familiar tools of graphics and “talking heads.” Tops in this category is “Wall Street Week,” the financial-news roundup that is one of the most watched programs on the entire public-television schedule. It is shown Fridays at 8:30 P.M. The host and guiding spirit is Louis Rukeyser, who started the series nearly a decade ago after being frustrated as an ABC-TV economics editor. At that time, his bosses felt viewers weren’t very interested in business news. In a way, “Wall Street Week” was Rukeyser’s revenge, eventually earning him a reported $500,000 a year. More important, sticking closely to a rigid format, he demonstrated that there was an appetite “out there” for discussions about cash flows and puts-and-calls.

text: For the moment, the hardest job in the Reagan Administration belongs to David Stockman, the young budget director. How shall the budget be cut? It’s up to him to figure out which agencies should be chopped off at the knees and which should sacrifice merely a finger or two. There are, naturally, no volunteers. But in a period of boiling inflation, the budget must be cut and the man with the hatchet deserves, if not sympathy, at least suggestions of the most important priorities. Here is the most important one: hunger.</br></br>Robert Kennedy helped mobilize the country against hunger, but not many remember that it was Richard Nixon who pledged to end hunger in America. In a decade, the nation has done just that. A medical team toured the country in 1969 and found widespread hunger and malnutrition. A similar survey in 1979 found that malnutrition has substantially disappeared. America has hung a safety net under society. It is called food stamps.</br></br>Some conservatives ridicule throwing money at social problems. But food stamps — coupons that poor people can use to buy food with—have fed the hungry. Food stamps, and associated programs, may be the overarching social achievement of our era. This year, the nation will spend $11 billion on stamps to help feed 22 million people, one American in ten.</br></br>Yet what are the noises now coming out of the Administration? Alarm; fear that this very growth denotes waste, fraud, freeloaders. It is said that food stamps are among the first things to cut in the budget, saving billions. It is said that all must share the burden. What that means is, let’s cut holes in the bottom of the safety net.</br></br>How can those who use food stamps do their “share”? Some recipients can give up all their stamps, or all of them can give up some stamps. Reducing eligibility standards could reduce participation by cutting off the “richest” of the poor. But who are they? Mostly they are elderly sick people or the working poor, precisely the kind of people the Reagan Administration wishes to support.

text: People who made profits on stocks last year— and there was ample opportunity with the sharp run-up in the stock market during the final days — may be able to spare some of their earnings from taxes by taking advantage of the favorable capital gains deduction.</br></br>plex, and taxpayers often are chagrined to discover that a minor miscalculation about the timing requirements that determine whether a gain is longterm or short-term can result in a major difference in the taxes owed.</br></br>First, there is the question of which items are considered capital assets. The general rule is that all properties are capital assets if not specifically excluded. In addition to stocks, bonds and securities, property used for personal purposes — a home, automobile, jew- elry, furniture and clothing — are considered capital assets. But excluded items — inventory, stock in trade, real estate or depreciable property used in a business, copyrights, business accounts or notes receivable and obligations of governmental bodies — are not.</br></br>Although the Government requires that the profit from the sale of personal property be duly reported, it apparently does not believe that turnabout is fair play. Deductions for losses on the sale of personal property are barred, unless the property was primarily used for business or investment purposes.</br></br>Thus, someone who takes a beating on the sale of a diamond ring bought for personal adornment cannot claim a loss even if the purchase was thought to be a safer investment than real estate; but the loss would be allowed if it could be shown that the ring was bought to make a profit, even if it was also worn occasionally.

text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 9 — Producer prices for finished goods, slowed by a drop in food prices, rose only five-tenths of 1 percent last month, providing another sign of the general decline in the rate of inflation this year.</br></br>The increase in the index, which measures prices of finished goods, generally at the wholesale level, was below the six-tenths of 1 percent rise in October, but well above the increases of one-tenth of 1 percent in August and two-tenths of 1 percent in September. The November increase amounts to 6 percent a year, before compounding.</br></br>Thus far this year, producer prices have increased only 7.4 percent, a rate that almost guarantees that 1981 will be the first year of single-digit inflation for producer prices since 1978. In addition, unless there is a very large and unexpected increase this month, this year’s rate will be the lowest since</br></br>Though November's increase exceeded those of August and September, the quick drop of the economy into the second recession in two years is expected to keep the downward pressure on inflation. At the same time, the unemployment rate is expected to approach or exceed 9 percent, the post-World War II record.</br></br>“The numbers suggest that we are continuing to make moderate but steady progress in bringing down inflation,” said Larry Speakes, the deputy White House press secretary. text: INTEREST rates again dominated all commodity futures markets last week as traders watched the banks’ prime lending rates settle at 20 percent, dashing many traders’ hopes for an easing of bank credit. The most active Treasury-bond delivery, the near March, fell to 70 and ll-32ds last Friday from 71 and 28-32ds a week earlier.</br></br>Because each 32d represents $31.25 per contract of $100,000 face value, the loss on the March delivery, 49-32ds, totaled $1,531.25.
