text: FROM the point of view of stopping inflation, the American economy is both too competitive and too monopolistic. Consider the 1979 inflationary facts of life. During the course of that year, productivity (output per hour of work) fell 2 percent and rising OPEC oil prices took 2 percent of the American gross national product. This meant that we could only have a nonin-flationary society in 1980 if the average American's income fell 4 percent.</br></br>Wages (and other incomes) must fall 2 percent to reflect the fact that American workers are 2 percent less efficient. If wages don’t fall, prices must go up 2 percent to cover the new, higher labor costs. But there must also be a counterbalance to the price rise in imported oil. This can only happen if there is an additional fall in wages.</br></br>The 4 percent cut in wages does not emerge from liberal or conservative economics, it is a simple matter of algebraic necessity. As long as productivity continues to fall and imported oil prices continue to rise, wages must fall if America is to have price stability.</br></br>If our economy were a perfectly competitive atomistic economy where every market operated on simple supply and demand, the necessary wage reduction would occur automatically as long as the Federal Reserve Board held the money supply constant.</br></br>Since competitive companies have no power to raise prices, they would have no choice but to cut employee wages when productivity fell. Similarly, employees would have no choice but to accept the cuts, or be replaced.

text: President Reagan’s economic program is fatally flawed because his passion for military strength directly conflicts with his goal of economic recovery. As Mr. Reagan said during the Presidential campaign, continued deficit spending can only mean higher inflation and a weak economy.</br></br>His military plans not only break the budget, they also violate important cautions cited by some leading economists. text: The Federal Reserve announced yesterday that the nation’s basic money supply fell $1.3 billion in the week ended July 1, and has now declined for two consecutive months.</br></br>The slowdown in growth of the money supply since April, when the adjusted M-1B measure grew at a 16.9 percent annual rate, has strengthened the already widespread predictions that the Fed has decided to encourage more money supply growth by making bank reserves slightly more plentiful.</br></br>“For the first time in three months the Fed is below or else hitting its growth targets for the two key money supply numbers,” said Allan Leslie, a money market analyst at the Discount Corporation of New York, a government securities dealer. “It’s very positive news for the credit markets,” Mr. Leslie added, “since over time you can be expecting the Fed to increase its targets for growth of nonborrowed reserves in the banking system.”</br></br>Before the money supply announcement interest rates declined in yesterday’s trading, as the Fed added reserves to the banking system for the third consecutive day when it arranged temporary purchases of securities. The Fed’s moves this week to add reserves were greater than some specialists expected, and combined with a drop in the overnight funds rate to as low as 17i/2 percent, it led them to conclude that the Fed was trying to make reserves slightly more plentiful.</br></br>Reserves are funds that banks and other financial institutions must maintain at the Fed or other regulators. When the Fed makes bank reserves less scarce, short-term interest rates decline, and money supply growth is stimulated as banks step-up their lending activity. When the Fed makes reserves scarcer, short-term interest rates rise, and money supply growth is curbed as banks cut back their lending activity.

text: IT has only taken six months for the Reagan economic program to fail in its promise of full employment and low inflation for 1982. Now, beset by inflationary fiscal deficits and the highest interest rates since F.D.R., the program instead has given the economy the current recession. How and why this happened is the subject of the fascinating article in the December issue of The AUantic Monthly, entitled, “The Education of David Stock-man,” by William Greider.</br></br>Much has been made of that article as a kiss and tell on the secret and devious goals of the Reagan plan. Scandal evaporates on a second reading, however, as it becomes clear that the greater concern should be with the sequence of steps that led to the failure of the program. What makes it so fascinating is that Mr. Greider and Mr. Stockman may know that sequence but are not telling the causes for failure.</br></br>Before the inauguration, the new economic team realized that it had to do the impossible in increasing defense spending, cutting taxes and balancing the budget, all at the same time. Mr. Stockman tells of two economic theories as two ways of solving the dilemma. The first theory denied the necessity of balancing the budget and the second denied the impossibility thereof. Supply-side economics denied balancing the budget was necessary by arguing that the tax cut would add more to the supply of capital than the unbalancing of the budget would subtract. And after all, increased investment for more capital was a way of increasing growth of output and reducing inflation.</br></br>Denying the impossibility of balancing the budget required more economic theory than that. The budget could be balanced if the tax cuts were small and defense spending held within limits. But there would also have to be deep cuts in domestic programs. If this cutting effort were recognized by investors and consumers, then the restoration of private-sector confidence would result in more gross national product and more taxes that would eliminate the deficit.</br></br>Paul W. MacAvoy is Frederick William Beinicke Professor of Economics at Yale University and was a member of President Ford’s Council of Economic Advisers.

text: Leading economists echo President Reagan’s assessment that the economy will remain “soggy” in the coming months, but they also wam that continuing high interest rates and the specter of inflationary Government deficits will hamper the President’s recovery program well "beyond the near-term.</br></br>The economists say that until these negative factors are removed, the economy will remain stagnant, despite the cut in tax rates. And they are not impresssed by some of the recent positive economic indicators.</br></br>“The economy has really gone nowhere since the first quarter of 1979,” said Alan Reynolds, chief economist for Polyconomics Inc., a private consulting firm. “I don’t think we are going to get out of this trap until we get a credible long-term monetary policy which will ensure the purchasing power of the dollar over the years. ’ ’ “The tax cut,” he added, “will give a little kick, but it won’t be enough to overcome our monetary disorder. There aren’t too many investments, or even personal decisions like cars, that warrant the current financing costs. What can you profitably do with 21 percent money?” “I don’t think we have the makings of a reasonable expansion for months to come,” said Walter Heller, former economic adviser to President Kennedy and President Johnson.</br></br>Where the Indicators Point “Even with the tax cut and the investment stimuli,” he added, “businessmen are worried about the huge budget deficits as far as the eye can see. That is what is holding back their confidence. text: FRANKFURT, Aug, 3 — Karl Otto Pohl, the president of the Bundesbank, West Germany’s central bank, has urged the Bonn Government to spend less time criticizing high United States interest rates, and more time putting its “own house in order.’’</br></br>He advised Bonn’s economic planners that such an emphasis was necessary to bring an early end to West Germany’s recession and meaningful improvement in the current-account deficit.</br></br>Mr. Pohl, in an interview Friday, one day after the Bonn Government disclosed a program of sharp spending cuts in its 1982 budget, said falling interest rates in the United States would not necessarily bring about lower rates in West Germany, "if, at the same time, America’s inflation dropped, and the country’s economic revival program” took effect.</br></br>Mr. Pohl praised the program of sharp spending cuts announced last week by the Bonn Government for its 1982 budget but warned that a Government economic recovery plan financed by increased taxes — a plan that is still under discussion in Bonn — would be counterproductive.</br></br>Mr. Pohl cautioned that Europe would be unable to insulate itself from the effects of United States inflation, with the recessionary effects it would bring, if Mr. Reagan’s policies failed.

text: The United States appears to be in a recession, but it may not last long or be severe, the Conference Board said yesterday in a newsletter.</br></br>Albert T. Sommers, chief economist of the business research organization, said America’s real output rate would probably decline slightly in the third quarter of 1981, compared with the second quarter, and would drop more sharply in the last quarter of the year. The forecast appeared in The Sommers Letter, issued every two weeks.</br></br>Mr. Sommers also said that a significant drop was possible in the more narrow measure of industrial production in the fourth quarter. The broader measure of output includes services, utilities and other items as well as industrial production.</br></br>The Conference Board’s analysis asserts that the traditional method of defining recession — two consecutive quarters of decline in real output—“is only barely useful.” The newsletter says: “Recession is a process, and it is only because it is a process that its beginning can be identified and its probable severity appraised. The process is the cumulative spreading of weaknesses from involved sectors to previously uninvolved sectors, working along the lines of the infinitely complex supply connections among industries, and the steplike interplays between changes in output, on the one hand, and changes in the incomes gen-</br></br>"Once recession satisfying this definition has begun, the originating causes of weakness — in this case prohibitively high interest rates — lose some of the relevance. True recession runs on its own internal energies. Even reversals in the originating causes — in this instance, a reversal into a significant decline of interest rates—are unlikely to have much effect for a considerable period. ” Mr. Sommers said further analysis may show that the current recession began in August, when unemployment began to rise, reaching 7.2 percent. text: IS the effort of the Federal Reserve to check inflation by holding down the rate of money supply growth a wrongheaded policy that actually destabilizes the economy by forcing up interest rates and accelerating velocity, the rate at which the money supply turns over?</br></br>This is the issue dramatized by the startling re-suits of this year’s first quarter when real gross national product climbed at an annual rate of 8.4 percent and nominal G.N.P. (total national output unadjusted for inflation) soared at a near-record rate of</br></br>The latest issue of the Quarterly Review of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York notes that “the unsettled conditions in the bond market resulting from the uncertainty about inflation occurred even as the narrow monetary aggregates weakened considerably during the first three months of the year. ’ ’ The Fed calculates that, adjusted for NOW accounts, which were introduced nationwide on Dec. 31. 1980, M-1A (currency plus demand deposits) did not increase at all in the first quarter and M-1B (M-1A plus checkable deposits at banks and thrift institutions) increased at an annual rate of only 1.1 percent. This meant that the income velocity of money (using M-1B as the base) soared by nearly 18 percent in the first quarter, more than offsetting the slowdown in the money supply.</br></br>Was this a fluke? Or does the first-quarter result, though more dramatic than in past periods when velocity increases offset reductions in the money supply, nevertheless signify a basic flaw of “practical monetarism,” the doctrine that has governed Fed policy since October 1979. The doctrine holds that by trying to control the money supply by regulating member-bank reserves, while essentially letting interest rates fluctuate as they will, the Fed can regulate nominal G.N.P. and slow the rate of inflation.</br></br>Almarin Phillips of the University of Pennsylvania, a leading monetary economist, thinks the first-quarter result was no fluke at all, but rather that monetarism as practiced by the Fed and other central banks suffers from the fatal flaw of disregarding velocity changes. “If the conventional and usually implicit view that velocity does not respond enough to offset quantitative controls is incorrect,” Professor Phillips says, "the basic paradigm of modem central banking and monetary policy is incorrect. ”

text: OF all the economic developments during the last three years, the decline of inflation has been one of the most dramatic and welcome. text: IN November, the voters of Nassau County will be asked to accept or reject a reallocation of weighted votes assigned to the members of its Board of Supervisors based not on population but on a distribution of “voting power” worked out by a computer.</br></br>Weighted voting in local government has long been in disrepute, and after the United States Supreme Court’s "one man, one vote” decision in 1964, it was abandoned by every state except New York. Even in New York, all the larger counties turned to representative county legislatures elected from equal population districts or a combination of single- and multi-member districts.</br></br>In 1967 the New York State Court of Appeals held weighted voting to be constitutional, provided a county could show through computer analysis that a supervisor’s share of the “voting power” was proportional to his unit’s share of the population. A unit’s “voting power” was equated to the number of times a change of its vote on an issue would change the final outcome of the board vote, based on a random fall of yes /no votes.</br></br>Under this ruling, votes were to be weighted not on the basis of population but according to a computerized analysis of the mathematical probabilities in an infinite number of random votes. However, the unit’s percentage of the total vote was to be approximately equal to its percentage of the total population.</br></br>This complex system, derived from the case of Reynolds v. Sims, sought to express in terms of percentages the discrepancy between “an ideal district and an actual voting district” established by a local plan. Under the Federal court's decision, discrepancies were to be expressed as percentages of deviation from the ideal for each district based on that district’s population.

text: Last week, the United States Gold Commission issued a report based on more than eight months of study that formally rejected a return to the gold standard. Following are excerpts from the section on domestic monetary arrangements, and comments by commission members.</br></br>WE considered a number of alternatives that would serve to reintroduce gold into our domestic monetary policy arrangements. The objective would be to improve monetary control through the discipline of gold for the purpose of reducing inflation. Linking changes in the growth rate of money or of some component of money, such as Federal Reserve notes, or of bank reserves, to the change in the gold stock is one approach which was considered for imposing the discipline of gold.</br></br>One way to reintroduce gold would be to require the Federal Reserve System to maintain a minimum ratio between the Government’s gold stock and the Federal Reserve monetary base (i.e., Federal Reserve notes plus bank reserves) or some monetary aggregate. A variant would fix upper and lower limits to the ratio, so that the System would be required to take expansionary actions when the ratio was at its lower limit. The gold cover requirement might be valued at the price of $42.22, or adjusted gradually, or allowed to fluctuate with market prices.</br></br>Along traditional gold-standard lines, the United States could define the dollar as a specified weight of gold (that is, fix the price of gold), set gold cover requirements for the Federal Reserve System, and allow the value of the gold stock to be determined by domestic and international gold flows. If the value of the gold stock rose through an inflow of gold, the Federal Reserve would be required to undertake actions to expand the money stock. If the value of the gold stock declined, it would be required to take contractionary actions.</br></br>Most members of the Commission believe that a return to the gold standard is not desirable. Even if that were not our view, for most of us there are two major problems in contemplating the feasibility of a return to a domestic gold standard. One is the absence of a sound guide on how to determine the fixed dollar price of gold at which resumption of a gold cover requirement could be introduced. The other one is the absence of a sound guide on the extent of feasible convertibility of domestic dollar obligations.

text: WASHINGTON, Feb. 10 — Following are excerpts from testimony of Paul A. Volcker, chairman of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, today before the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs:</br></br>As you know, the economy has been in recession for some months. The recession has some of the characteristics of earlier downturns. But it seems to me plainly wrong to think of the current state of the economy as simply reflecting “another” recession.</br></br>Rather, we are seeing the culmination of a much longer period of unsatisfactory economic performance extending well back into the 1970’s — performance marked by poor productivity, growing unemployment, much higher interest rates, and pressures on the real earnings of the average citizen and on the real profits of our businesses.</br></br>A number of factors have contributed to that deterioration in our performance, not all of them completely understood. But one pervasive element — an element particularly relevant to monetary policy — stands out:. We found ourselves in the midst of the most prolonged inflation in our history, and that inflationary process had come to feed on itself. Incentives were distorted. Too much of the energy of our citizens was directed toward seeking protection from future price increases and toward speculative activity, and too little toward production. Increasingly depressed and volatile capital markets reflected the uncertainties. Effective tax rates increased as inflation carried taxpayers into higher brackets. But, in a sluggish economy, those revenues did not keep up with our spending plans and programs.</br></br>Against that background, the notion that we might comfortably live with inflation — or that we could accept inflation in the interest of strong growth — was exposed as an Illusion. I believe it is fair to say a clear national consensus emerged that turning back inflation had to be a top priority of economic policy — that a stable dollar is a necessary part of the foundation of a strong economy.

text: SREAD the headlines about the creeping unemployment rate, mergers, plant closings, layoffs, consolidations and corporate staff reductions with a strange feeling. Free-lancing helped make ends meet but the basic question remained. Will 1 ever find regular employment again? Being one of those greater New York minority members, the sole breadwinner for spouse, family and mortgage banker, the question had a very real ring.</br></br>And, it is personal. It works on your mind, your personality, your being. Is it me or the situation? A perennial question. Fill in the answer of your choice at your discretion. I’m concerned that many won’t get jobs • until the summer.”

text: Slowing the rise in prices has been “a painful success,” says a key Presidential adviser. But how long will it last?</br></br>THE outstanding achievement of President Reagan's economic policy this year is the dramatic slowing of inflation. For the first time since the late 1960’s, inflation is clearly on the run: • In the last year, every major price index compiled by the Federal Government has sharply slowed its rate of rise and raw commodity prices have actually fallen.</br></br>• In the midst of the critical Christmas shopping season, many of the nation’s leading retailers are cutting prices. The rest are holding prices flat or raising them far more slowly than in the past.</br></br>• In spite of a recent flurry of union resistance to concessions, there has been a widespread slowdown in the upward movement of wages over the past few years. That has taken some of the upward pressure off prices.</br></br>Moreover, the end of the good tidings is not in sight. Though most analysts expect the elusive economic recovery to begin sometime next year, they say that the rise in consumer prices should hold to this year’s expected 5 percent even after business begins to pick up.

text: THE recent decline in interest rates and the expected forthcoming economic recovery are supposed to be good news for manufacturers of mobile homes as well as the rest of the housing industry.</br></br>For builders of “manufactured housing,” as mobile homes are called in the industry, the growth prospects related to an improved economy are only part of the story. “Keeping housing affordable is the main objective,” said Robert Curran, an analyst at Merrill Lynch & Company. “Interest rates are likely to stay high, so there will be continuing efforts to downsize housing. The industry is moving in the direction of more off-site manufacturing of homes and components.”</br></br>The idea of reducing the cost of manufacturing housing at central locations rather than on-site is not new. There have been enough disappointments in the past to make skeptics say that “the mobile home business has a great future, and always will.” But now, some analysts are convinced that the industry is attractive as a long-term investment as well as during the expansion expected in the coming growth stage of the housing cycle.</br></br>Analysts at Value Line, for example, have assigned the industry their fifth-highest rating for timeliness, out of 93 industries rated weekly. text: DETROIT, June 26 — Along with all the other miseries of the recession, people who live in the states hit worst by it are also paying for the economic slump in another way: through higher personal taxes.</br></br>An analysis of tax increases passed by a number of states in the Great Lakes and Pacific Northwest regions showed that individual taxpayers were assuming a growing share of their state's expenses. This is partly because tax revenue from businesses usually declines when the economy slows, but mainly because the income and sales taxes adapted by hard-pressed states and municipalities have fallen most heavily on individual taxpayers.</br></br>The income tax is generally the most tempting source of revenue for states that face growing deficits and a need to raise large amounts of new money, amounts that such "easy” taxes as new duties on cigarettes and liquor do not yield.</br></br>"The states that are really bleeding because of the recession almost have no choice but to go to the income tax, because that’s where the real money is,” said John Shannon, the taxation and finance specialist at the Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations, a public policy research group in Washington, D.C.</br></br>“I would say, as a guess, that between 70 and 90 percent of the dollars from these taxes would fall on individuals,” Mr. Shannon added. “For one thing, the last thing these states want to do is develop a reputation that they’re bad for business. ’’

text: WASHINGTON, Dec. 13 — The Federal Reserve Board, in a move intended to stimulate the long-awaited economic recovery, today cut its key lending rate to 8'/2 percent from 9 percent, effective Tuesday.</br></br>The reduction in the discount rate, which is the interest the Federal Reserve charges on loans it makes to banks and other financial institutions, was the seventh since July, when the discount rate was 12 percent.</br></br>Other interest rates have also fallen several points since then, in response, and analysts said that the latest cut meant that short-term rates, including the prime rate, could soon drop by half a percentage point.</br></br>Some analysts said that the Federal Reserve’s action today shows that it is trying to force down interest rates to deal with the persisting recession, rather than follow its usual practice of cutting the discount rate only after short-term interest rates decline in the financial markets.</br></br>“What it shows is that, in the eyes of the Federal Reserve, we do not yet have a recovery in the economy and they are moving again to start the economy,” said Allen Sinai of Data Resources Inc., an economic consulting concern. “Here’s a situation where the Fed is aggressively leading interest rates down,” he added. Today’s cut also ap- peared to reflect a concern about strains on the international financial structure, some analysts said, noting that the action could indirectly lessen the debt burden on the world’s developing nations by reducing interest rates on that debt. The action comes as the United States and other countries are working on a new $1.5 billion line of credit to Brazil so that it can continue fulfilling its loan obligations.

How it fell into this predicament, and some indications of how book people are trying to find a way out, are suggested by three conventions held by the American Booksellers Association during the past three decades.</br></br>• In 1950,650 booksellers and publishers got together over a June weekend at New York’s Hotel As tor. Before and after panel discussions on the problems of operating a bookstore, booksellers browsed at tables edging the hotel’s grand ballroom on which publishers displayed the most promising of 10,000 titles being issued that year. Except for several houses in Boston and Philadelphia and a sprinkling of university presses across the country, virtually all American book publishing was concentrated in Manhattan and 40 percent of all the nation’s sales were in the Northeast, so New York seemed to be a natural place for the meeting. The cozy, rather provincial affair received scant attention from the press.</br></br>• Last year, 17,000 booksellers, publishers, authors and agents from every section of the United States and many foreign lands congregated over four May days in a vast convention center in Anaheim, Calif., the home of Disneyland. California then accounted for 20 percent of the nation's book sales, as much as the Northeast. Many large New York-based houses that displayed their publications in dazzling exhibits were owned by large corporations listed on the stock exchanges; little wonder that the business press reported what transpired. Many of the social affairs were graced by stars of show business and politics; little wonder that television and newspapers covered the events. Before the year was over, it was said, 40,000 books would be Issued. But in guarded tones. Insiders traded talk of list-cutting, imminent mergers of publishing houses and the possibility that many talented old hands would soon be unemployed.</br></br>• Last month, when the A.B.A. convened in Dallas, the mood was quite subdued. Only 15,000 book people showed up for the affair and they seemed a bit lost in the Texas-size convention center. Although the press focused its attention on the dramatic performances of several actresses-tumed-author, the real news was elsewhere. Many of the houses exhibiting the most promising of this year’s 50,000 titles were young, small and had about them the air of a small cottage industry. There were many displays of books and electronic software to be used with computers. The best attended and liveliest meetings were discussions of the relationship of books and computers in the future.</br></br>The changes that transformed the book world over this period mirrored changes in the nation's economic and social life. Shortly after World War II, for the first time, the book became a medium for the masses. Millions of middle-class and blue-collar Americans, who had previously relied on lending libraries and popular magazines for their reading, bought books, thanks to the paperback revolution. Paperbacks first appeared in 1939 when Pocket Books introduced soft-cover reprints of hard-cover books. The 25-cent price of those early paperbacks made the lending libraries’ 5-cents-a-day charge seem costly.

text: Though Ronald Reagan came to office preaching slogans about big, bad deficits, what he’s preaching now is responsible fiscal policy. Forget the deficit, he says, until Government can steer the economy out of recession.</br></br>Yet when it comes to social policy, the President suddenly remembers the deficit. What we must do is get the economy restored on a long-term, permanent basis. And everything we do must be directed toward that. ”</br></br>Everything we do. That’s not only right; it’s brave. Consider how dramatically Mr. Reagan inveighed against the deficit two years ago. The national debt, he said, was approaching $1 trillion. “If you had a stack of thousand-dollar bills in your hand only 4 inches high, you’d be a millionaire. A trillion dollars would be a stack of thousand-dollar bills 67 miles high.”</br></br>The President knows that in two years the stack has risen to 80 miles. With a $200 billion deficit now likely, it could climb another 13 miles this year alone. text: THE Federal Reserve’s 1983 game plan reveals two important changes In monetary policy making. If the money supply provided a dependable guide to that impact, no additional yardstick would be necessary.</br></br>But lately the money supply has been an unreliable guide. text: WASHINGTON — It should have been one of Ronald Reagan’s best weeks. The stock market closed at new highs amid spreading euphoria that economic recovery had begun at last. text: A SUBJECT that is bound to attract increased scrutiny and analysis among economists as the nation's . economic recovery' progresses is the question of the adequacy of current productive capacity in key American industries. text: Over the years, periodic tax cuts of the sort being debated in Washington have served an important but often unstated subsidiary purposes—offsetting the impact of inflation, the silent tax collector.</br></br>It is well recognized that inflation, by raising nominal incomes and eroding personal exemptions, steadily sweeps taxpayers into higher brackets. Tax increases outstrip real income gains, and for some taxpayers, taxes go up while real income stands still.</br></br>But according to the Advisory Commission on Intergovernmental Relations, the four major tax cuts between 1960 and 1975 left taxpayers in Che aggre--gate better off than if Congress had enacted an automatic inflation adjustment instead. They paid taxes in -1975 at an average effective rate of 11.4 percent, compared with 12.3 percent if instead the 1960 income tax structure had been indexed to factor out inflation.</br></br>The advisory panel expects that "for ,the foreseeable future," Congress will have the fiscal wherewithal to rebate the "inflation tax" by enacting periodic tax reductions. But the advisory commission, a 26-member group drawn from Federal, state and local governments, does not favor a policy of ad hoc tax cuts. The commission has become a leading advocate of indexing both Federal and state or local income taxes to filter out inflation.</br></br>Last August, the advisory commission urged Congress to adopt an annual adjustment of personal exemptions, low-income allowances, the standard deduction ceiling and tax rate brackets. text: WASHINGTON — When a bill to provide $4 billion In public works jobs came to the Senate floor recently as part of the new Administration's stimulus plan, there was little disagreement about the total but a great deal of disagreement about how to distribute it among the states. Ultimately, although the purpose of the bill was to relieve areas with severe unemployment, in order to muster a majority of Senators the statistical definition of "severe” had to be relaxed so that more states would qualify for funds, and each state had to be guaranteed a minimum allocation of $30 million whether it needed it or not.</br></br>The incident was a classic example of the wonderland of Federal grant-in-aid formulas,, in which ostensible national objectives—such as fighting poverty, educating children, or promoting mass transit—become blurred in the attempt to gain legislative support for the funding necessary to achieve them. Rather than disinterestedly deciding who are the poorest, the hungriest or the most in need of mass transit funds, a member of Congress tends to vote for the distribution formulas that benefit his own constitutents the most. The struggle over these formulas pits section against section, and urban legislators against rural.</br></br>_In the end, the formula is determined by what is necessary to produce a successful coalition. Senator Abraham Ribicoff, Democrat of Connecticut, described the process during the debate on the jobs bill. The Senator said, “Day in and day out on this floor all of us get these sheets of paper [with various proposed formulas], and everybody fiddles around with a formula to find out . . . whether it will give a dollar more to 26 states, and then you become a winner—and then the national interest is forgotten.” More often than not, the losers in recent years have been the states of the highly urbanized industrial Northeast.</br></br>give a rural bias to the Federal formulas and channeled a disproportionate amount of aid into the southeastern states, said Sally W. Swartzmiller, an economist in the New York State Budget Division. “But to make doubly sure that the funds for material and child health, crippled children’s services and child welfare services went into rural areas, the number of rural children and the number of rural live births were counted twice for part of the distribution.” Similarly, Federal aid to education is based on the number of children between the ages of 5 and 17 in families with incomes below the poverty level, currently $5,780 for a family of four. Welfare payments are counted as income. In New York City, many hard-pressed families are above the national poverty level, partly because the welfare payments, reflecting the cost of living, are higher in the Northeast than in other sections of the country.</br></br>The original revenue sharing bill, in 1972, also illustrated how formula factors can produce disparities among regions. The bill provided more aid Tor areas without plumbing facilities and with a large number of persons per room. Northern Senators pointed out that most buildings without adequate plumbing were in the South, and that lack of heat was a more appropriate index of poor living conditions in the North. Overcrowding, they said, is also far more prevalent in the South than in the North, where a family of four in the Bronx might live in a six room apartment, albeit unheated and rat-infested. As a result of these objections, plumbing was dropped from the formula, but overcrowding, defined as a housing unit with 1.01 persons or more per room, remains a factor that brings some places more aid. Similar compromises had to be accepted to obtain Federal aid for mass transit. To get the legislation through Congress, members from New York agreed to a formula that was based on population and density rather than on the number of riders. text: WASHINGTON—From the staff of Congress and from the economists at the Brookings Institution have recently come sober assessments about inflation. It is, they say, a deeply entrenched force in the American economy, and, they maintain, the Carter Administration has not come up with an anti-inflation policy that is likely to make much of a difference.</br></br>"The outlook for inflation is not encouraging," Brookings, a liberal research organization, said earlier this month. "The deepest and longest recession since 1938 has not reduced the underlying inflation rate of 5-6 percent a year.. .. The general rate of inflation will not be greatly moderated by the policies proposed by the new Administration.” Few in government would disagree with that assessment of the underlying rate: The stubborn persistence of that rate is one reason Federal Reserve chairman Arthur F. Burns expressed concern about last week's slide in the dollar, provoked by the release of June’s record trade deficit figure. A weak dollar, Mr. Burns noted, generates inflation by increasing prices for imported goods.</br></br>Why is inflation so persistent? What is the Carter Administration doing to combat it, what is it not doing and why?</br></br>The answer to the first question sheds some light on the next two. Despite the existence of idle resources and labor, costs and prices defy the laws of economics and chase each other up. That is in large part because expectations of inflation tend to be self-fulfilling. As the Congressional Budget Office put it in its recent report: "During the last decade, inflation has become embedded strongly in our economic machinery. The rapid spread of cost-of-living-adjusted labor contracts, the reflection of inflationary expectations in a broad spectrum of interest rates and the automatic linking of major Federal entitlement programs to consumer price increases are a few important examples."</br></br>In 1976, Jimmy Carter gave indications that he would actively seek to break inflationary psychology. As a candidate from the South wooing the liberal northern wing of the Democratic party, Jimmy Carter said he was for stand-by wage-price controls; as President, he has proved to be anything as an activist on the wage-price front.

text: WASHINGTON, April 15—Following are excerpts from a statement on inflation issued today by President Carter:</br></br>The anti-inflation program is tailored to the nature, of the problems we face. It has three basic parts:</br></br>Federal economic and budgetary policies that promote growth while avoiding overstimulation; specific governmental actions to fight inflation; and a voluntary effort by business, labor and Government to achieve our common objectives of providing jobs, promoting steady growth and controlling inflation.</br></br>By any objective measure, the economy has ample room to expand without running into excess demand. Yet many people fear that current budgetary policies will lead to renewed inflationary pressures. I want to address those fears directly.</br></br>Inadequate tax revenues from a stagnant economy—not legitimate Federal spending programs—are the principal source of the deficits. We have large budget deficits today because recovery from the worst recession in 140 years is still incomplete. As the recovery proceeds, the deficits must shrink and eventually disappear. The combined total of private and public demands on the economy must not be allowed to exceed our productive capacity, or inflation will surely be rekindled. I have made a firm commitment to have a balanced budget in a normal economy by F.Y.1981, and I intend to do everything I can to honor that commitment.

text: THE week’s economic and financial news seemed baffling, frustrating, even doublecrossing. The national economic indicators pointed up, but the stock market went down. The Commerce Department’s key index of leading indicators increased 0.4 percent in February, showing how early the economy began bouncing back from the severe winter freeze that had dropped the same index 1.2 percent in January.</br></br>The recovery was getting back into stride. Retail sales were up; factory orders were up; housing and construction contracts were up. Secretary of Commerce Juanita M. Kreps said she expected real gross national product in the first quarter to "hit just under 4 percent." Real G.N.P. in the January-March quarter had earlier been estimated to come in half a percentage point lower.</br></br>Mrs. Kreps and her economists might still be on the low side. Some private economists calculate that first-quarter G.N.P. may have climbed at an annual rate of about 4.5 percent. The April-June quarter, making up for the unusually rough winter, is likely to advance at an annual rate of 7 percent or more. The economy in the second half of 1977 promises to settle down to a 6 percent annual rate of gain.</br></br>Given the overhang of 7.3 percent unemployment— 7 million workers—and Mr. Carter’s commitment to get unemployment down, which was the main plank in his economic campaign platform, the President is not going to be talked out of his stimulus program by the conservatives’ argument that the economy is moving fast enough, or too fast, already. The jobless rate is still likely to be too high by the end of 1977, even with the fiscal stimulus.</br></br>Yet, where Washington sees itself as cautiously prodding along a fairly good but still inadequate recovery (inadequate to kick off capital spending or reduce joblessness fast enough), Wall Street fears the fiscal hypodermic needle. It fears worsening inflation and climbing interest rates—perceived as poison for the securities markets.

text: REACTION to President Carter's anti-inflation program varies greatly among different interest groups. Labor unions, with few exceptions, are opposed to the "voluntary’’ program. Murphy of the General Motors Corporation; have pledged to support the President’s anti-inflation program, even if it means an economic slowdown and lower profits. Wall Street, which is eager to see interest rates go down and stock prices go up, would accept sluggish growth and more unemployment to bring inflation under control.</br></br>Wealthy individuals have always been louder than poor people in denouncing inflation, and higher-income groups have helped to make the Republican Party more anti-inflationist than the Democratic Party, with its larger constituency among labor, blacks and other lower-income groups.</br></br>But how does this division square with the popular notion that inflation makes the rich richer and the poor poorer? text: WASHINGTON, July 27 (AP) — The decline in United States oil imports will continue for the remainder of this year and contribute to a lower trade deficit and a stronger dollar, Treasury Under Secretary Anthony M. text: New studies show that price rises affect capital gains more than income from wages. As the Government considers tax changes, it had better take that fact into account</br></br>Wage earners are acutely aware of the income tax bite in the paycheck. text: LOS ANGELES—This year, 600,000 teen-age boys will become unwed fathers. Until recently, they were ignored by social agencies and parents busy ooplng with the problems of unwed teen-age girls, who face a bleak future of unemployment and overwhelming responsibilities for child rearing.</br></br>Now, however, two pioneering social agencies in Southern California are counseling boys as well as girls because they have found that both partners in an out-of-wedlock pregnancy suffer guilt and anxiety that can lead to serious psychological problems if unresolved. The agencies also have discovered that involving the boy in the decision to keep or place the baby for adoption relieved the girl’s guilt and makes her adjustment much easier.</br></br>"In the past, society ignored the unwed teen-age father because it assumed that he was just sowing wild oats and didn’t care about the girl or their baby,” said Chuck Wilkersons. He is a social worker who has counceled unwed teen-age fathers for the past two years at the Children’s Home Society of Orange County, a private, non-sectarian child welfare organization. "The boy was encouraged to run away from his responsibilities because an out-of-wedlock pregnancy was assumed to be the girl’s problem,” he said.</br></br>Less than 5 percent of the unwed fathers who participate in the counseling programs at the Children’s Home Society come without being invited by the social workers. In most cases, the girl comes alone or with her parents for the first session. Many of the girls find out about the counseling programs through their friends, schools or the yellow pages.</br></br>“Initially, the girl and her family resist any effort to involve the boy in the counseling sessions because they feel that the boy is no good and has done enough damage,” said Mr. Wilker-son. "We point out to them that two of them were involved in the pregnancy and two of them should be involved in its resolution.”

text: 1 really did not expect to be back in the unemployment line so soon but after six months, I was filling out forms again with a potential employer. text: To defend the dollar, it has repeatedly been suggested, the United States ought to raise domestic interest rates to at-tract international capital, thereby off-setting the current, record trade deficit.</br></br>In fact, policies aimed at facilitating an outflow of capital, particularly to the developing and smaller industrialized countries, would contribute more to the dollar’s long-run defense!</br></br>Tighter money will indeed lead to a stronger dollar in the short run, but it will also choke off real growth and is likely to weaken the dollar in the longer run. Some economic forecasters already see the possibility of a credit crunch later this year, leading to a major recession in 1979, and the Federal Reserve’s defense of the dollar through high interest rates substantially increases the likelihood of a debilitating crunch.</br></br>The dollar’s current weakness does not stem from an inability to attract international capital: indeed, the United States is probably attracting too much capital for its state of development. During 1977, on a net basis, the United States borrowed about $20 billion overseas. Though much of these borrowings were involuntary, reflecting the efforts . to bolster the dollar through exchange-market intervention, some capital was attracted to the United States by the security of investment here and the relatively high rate of return.</br></br>The truth is that to achieve a more efficient worldwide allocation of resources, mature economies such as the United States ought to be net capital exporters—not capital importers. With the worldwide distribution of capital, labor and resources, the productivity of capital is higher in a number of other countries, including many of the developing nations, than in the United States.

text: The Wall Street Journal observed unhappily the other day that its editors had begun to fear “that the control of this inflation exceeds not only our will but our intellect."</br></br>This dire sentiment was accompanied by a survey of economists that showed a general consensus that inflation would continue well into the Eighties; several believed, however, without much solid evidence, that the American economy will have righted itself by the end of the next decade.</br></br>If so, it certainly won’t be because nature and the market were left to go their ways unmolested. If nothing else, continuing American dependence on imported oil obtained at OPEC prices will require direct action of some kind. The very occasion of the Journal’s despondence was its concern whether Chairman Paul Volcker and the Federal Reserve Board have sufficient power to “manage the world supply of dollars in such a way as to produce an acceptable level of stability.” (And that was before the dollar tumbled to $500 an ounce against gold.)</br></br>At risk of appearing to assert superior “intellect” to that of The Wall Street Journal, which Milton Friedman himself might tremble to do, the following are some steps that appear to me to be worth serious consideration in the Eighties — by no means offered as a “strategy” to fight inflation but only as individual actions that might be useful within such a strategy: 1. Strong oil conservation measures. Hobart Rowen of The Washington Post has pointed out, for example, that a computer-based coupon gasoline rationing system costing about $2 billion to operate could reduce consumption by 1.5 million barrels a day. At prospective oil prices, that would save $14 billion a year. To save as much by pricing would require a $1.50 tax per gallon of gasoline, running up other prices ruinously.</br></br>2. Selected controls. As a stopgap to allow time for long-term measures to be developed, price controls on such necessities as food and medical care would be of great help to most Americans. A more realistic wage standard (not one set at half the rate of inflation), with sharper teeth, toughly enforced, would have to accompany price controls.

text: In the last decade or so, the American economy has been undone by a series of bubbles. First there was the dot-com boom, in which start-ups without business models were suddenly worth billions of dollars. Then after a brief recession, we began speculating about real estate, so that Las Vegas tract homes tripled in value before they even had roofs. The latest suspect for a bubble is gold, which has doubled in price over the past three years.</br></br>Why are bubbles such a persistent feature of financial history? Economists argue that these speculative frenzies are caused in part by market failures like too much liquidity or lax regulation. Cognitive psychologists, meanwhile, see bubbles as a case of pattern recognition gone awry, as people extrapolate the past into the future. In recent years, neuroscientists also have become interested in 'bubbles, if only because the financial manias seem to take advantage of deep-seated human flaws; the market fails only because the brain fails first. Read Montague, at Baylor College of Medicine, has spent the last few years trying to decipher the bits of brain behind our irrational exuberance. It’s microeconomics at its most microscopic.</br></br>Montague’s experiments go like this: A subject is given $100 and some basic information about the stock market. After choosing how much money to invest, the player watches as his investments either rise or fall in value. The game continues for 20 rounds, and the subject gets to keep the money. One interesting twist is that instead of using random simulations of the market, Montague relies on real data from past markets, so people unwittingly “play” the Dow of 1929, the S&P 500 of1987 and the Nasdaq of1999. While the subjcctsare making their investment decisions, Montague measures the activity of neurons in the brain.</br></br>At first, Montague’s data confirmed the obvious: our brains crave reward. He watched as a cluster of dopamine neurons acted like greedy information processors, firing rapidly as the subjects tried to maximize their profits during the early phases of the bubble. When share prices kept going up, these brain cells poured dopamine into the caudate nucleus, which increased the subjects’ excitement and led them to pour more money into the market. The bubble was building.</br></br>But then Montague discovered something strange. As the market continued to rise, these same neurons significantly reduced their rate of firing. “It’s as if the cells were getting anxious," Montague say s.

text: IF you were going to turn to omy one economist to understand the problems facing the economy, there is little doubt that the economist would be John Maynard Keynes. Although Keynes died more than a half-century ago, Ills diagnosis of recessions and depressions remains tile foundation of modern macroeconomics. Ills insights go a long way toward explaining the challenges we now confront.</br></br>According to Keynes, the root cause of economic downturns is insufficient aggregate demand. When the total demand for goods and services declines, businesses throughout the economy see their sales fall off. Lower sales induce firms to cut back production and to lay off worker^. Rising unemployment and declining profits further depress demand, lending to a feedback loop with a very unhappy ending.</br></br>The situation reverses, Keynesian theory says, only when some event or policy increases aggregate demand.</br></br>Tlte economy's output of goods and services is traditionally divided into four components: consumption, investment, net exports and government purchases. Any expansion in demand lias to come from one of these four. But in. each case, strong forces are working to keep spending down. consumption The Conference Board reports that consumer confidence is near its record low. text: STRUGGLING as we are with the housing bust, the credit crunch, shrinking consumption, rising unemployment and fal-| tering business investment, we can be forgiven for thinking that all the big shoes have dropped. There is another one up there, however, and it is about to come down.</br></br>State and city governments have yet to shrink the economy; indeed, they have even managed to prop it up; They have quietly maintained their spending at pre-crisis levels even as they warn of numerous cutbacks forced on them by declining tax revenues. The cutbacks, however, are written into budgets for a fiscal year that begins on July 1, a month,away. In the meantime the states and cities, often drawing on rainy-day savings, have carried their share of the load for the national economy.</br></br>That share is gigantic. At $1.8 trillion annually in a $14 trillion economy, the states and municipalities spend almost twice as much as the federal government, including the cost of the Iraq war. When librarians, lifeguards, teachers, transit workers, road repair crews and health care workers disappear, or airport and school construction is halted, the economy trembles. None of that, or very little, has happened so far, not even in California, despite a significant decline in tax revenue.</br></br>"We are looking at a $4 billion cut to public schools and deep cuts that will result in thousands of Californians losing their health care," said Jean Ross, executive director of the California Budget Project, offering a preview of coming hardships. "But the reality is we have not pulled money off the streets yet.”</br></br>Quite the opposite, the states and municipalities have increased their spending in recent quarters, bolstering the nation’s meager economic growth. Over the past year, they have added $40 billion to their,outlays, even allowing for scattered spending freezes and a few cutbacks in advance of July 1. Total employment has also risen. But when the current fiscal year ends in 30 days (or in the fall for many municipalities), state and city spending will fall, along with employment — slowly at first and then quite noticeably after the next president takes office.

text: WHEN oil prices double or triple tn less than a year, that is a momentous event in America. Or at least it | nnce was The stock market would plunge The economy would slow, or fall into recession Presidents wearing sweaters would ask the public to turn thermostats down.</br></br>All this was standard in the 1970’s and 1980's, but no longer Oil has quietly lost its hold on the American economy.</br></br>If that sounds like an epitaph, let me soften it. Petroleum prices, which have more than doubled since last March, still have a little clout Gasoline prices arc higher, so is the pnce of heating oil Cargo rates and some airline fares have gone up The Consumer Price Index itself is rising at a 2 6 percent annual rate, up from 2 1 percent last spring Oil. directly or indirectly, accounts for all of the rise But 2 6 percent is pretty mild, and crude oil now appears to be edging down from its November peak of $28 a barrel “We have already seen the worst cf the inflationary impact, unless you think oil prices are going to double again, which no one does,” said David V/yss, chief economist at Standard & Poor’s DR I, a forecasting service. text: In a period of so much uncertainty, few people want to commit what may now be sharply depleted assets, especially when returns from relatively safe perches on the sidelines in cash or cash equivalents look pretty good Those returns look reasonable even after the Federal Reserve last week made its third rate cut of the year — and, given the way stocks have behaved, just keeping pace with inflation seems a minor triumph</br></br>Where to put your money while waiting out the storm depends on how much flexibility you want, whether you insist on having your money insured by the government, and just how willing you are to tolerate low but stable returns Some of the options are a throwback You can, of course, stick with a savings account at the local bank But such accounts pay relatively little, even compared with the chief alternatives, money market funds and and certificates of deposit Other than convenience, the main attraction is federal deposit insurance, for up to $100,000 an account</br></br>At Emigrant Savings Bank in New York, for instance, a savings account now earns 2 25 percent a year, according to John M Fall, a vice president The rate applies whether you request the traditional passbook that is still favored by older depositors or accounts that provide only monthly statements. The law, however, denies passbook users access to automated teller machines Where could you do better0 There is no central source for tracking savings account rates So to find the best deal, you have to go from bank to bank But keep fees in mind "You might have a better rate someplace," Mr Fall said, “but the fees could be higher " Emigrant charges $2 a month for accounts of less than $500, but this is waived if an individual has several accounts totaling more than that And savings accounts may offer check-writing privileges, typically limited to three checks a month Some online banks, like ING Direct, pay considerably higher interest, but not everyone wants to deal with an institution that has no physical office Savings accounts in general have few fans among experts “1 recommend against them because the interest rate tends to be low," said Scott M Kahan, a financial planner and president of the Financial Asset Management Corporation in New York.</br></br>For a better return, money market funds are probably the best bet "They are not guaranteed," said Harold Evensky, who heads the Evensky Group, a financial planner in Coral Gables, Fla. "But they pay higher rates than savings accounts, and they are considered extraordinarily safe ” Banks also offer money market deposit accounts — and they are insured — but the' yields are usually lower “Banks are not encouraging that business because they are not trying to build assets” by paying fully competitive rates, said Peter Crane, managing editor of iMoneyNet, which monitors money funds They can pay as little as 2 percent, though the average compounded seven-day return on money market funds tracked by hts firm is about 5 percent</br></br>"Look for a fund that does not have commercial paper,” the jou’s of corporations, said Bruce R Bent, chairman of the Reserve Funds, a money market sponsor "There have been instances where funds have held paper for institutions such as Pacific Gas and Electric that have defaulted In those cases, the funds made good the difference, but why ask for trouble0" While the vast majority of money market funds are fully taxable, there are those — holding about 12 percent of money market assets — that suck to tax-exempt securities. Because their returns now average only about 2 25 percent, they are aimed mainly at the well to do, said Connie Bugbee, editor of Money Fund Report, an industry publication "The average investor in the 28 percent or 31 percent tax bracket can earn higher after-tax rates in a taxable money fund," Ms Bugbee said

Nov. 4 — With daily doses of bad economic news pointing to the first recession In more than a decade, government policy makers face increasing questions about whether they have the resolve and the proper tools to bring about a auick recovery Just as the terrorist attacks required the United States to fight a new kind of war, economists said, the government faces an economic downturn that does not match previous scripts and that so far has not been particularly responsive to the combination of tax cuts and aggressive mterest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve Board.</br></br>Yet while the economy seemed to be crumbling from the delayed effects of a one-two punch — the bursting of the 1990’s bubble followed by the terrorist attacks on Sept 11 — Washington was dithering Even as the latest statistics showed that the economy had contracted over the summer and that unemployment had surged by half a percentage point in October, to 5 4 percent, the two parties in Congress and the Bush administration sank more deeply into an ideological bog over how to respond Republicans pushed their plan for another round of tax cuts that would largely benefit companies and upper-income people Democrats pressed for an approach that would give most help to the unemployed and those with lower incomes, and would rely in large part on increased government spending.</br></br>President Bush repeatedly called on the parties to bridge their differences and act but offered no new proposals of his own and defended his focus on tax cuts.</br></br>By the end of the week, they were clearly aware that their inability to get something done left them at risk of being seen as part of the problem rather than part of the solution.</br></br>“We’re seven weeks after the event," said Richard J DeKaser, chief economist at National City Bank in Cleveland, referring to the attacks, “and they’re still debating " “It is getting late," Mr. DeKaser added.

text: ■ With grand strategies and firm con-B victions becoming casualties of the stalled, often rocky stock market, some people on Wall Street are reviving a strategy intended to capitalize on such difficult conditions. The approach, called pair trading. is essentially an exercise m extreme stock-picking that seeks to make an investor indifferent to the which way the overall market goes — or whether it moves at all.</br></br>A pair trade means buying a stock that is thought to be undervalued while selling short an equal dollar amount of a similar or related stock, typically of a competitor, that appears overvalued.</br></br>The short position, which is a wager that the stock price will decline, reduces risk by protecting against a market downturn. Offsetting it with the stock that is owned — the long side of the equation — makes an investor neutral to the market and, depending on the picks, more or less impervious to the vicissitudes of a particular industry What’s left are bets on individual stocks.</br></br>If the stock picks are squarely on the mark, an investor can make money on both the long and short sides, and the direction of the the overall market does not matter.</br></br>“It’s actually an all-weather strategy, but it makes more sense in a sideways market,” said Christopher J. Wolfe, equity strategist for pnvate clients at J. P. Morgan Chase. “It works well with companies with similar products or end markets whose stocks are closely correlated, but where there is a valuation disparity.” “Pair trades also are a way to play volatility,” Mr. Wolfe said. That is because any development that strengthens the competitive position of one of the companies versus the other, like a new product, will have a greater impact on the respective stock prices m a volatile market “The correlations become less stable,” he said.

text: Yesterday the Federal Reserve lowered interest rates for the ninth time this year. The federal funds rate, the key tool of monetary policy, is now 2.5 percent — below the level of inflation. The Fed was hoping it would buoy investor and consumer confidence, and given the markets’ current psychology, it probably had little choice. The stock market did respond well to the move.</br></br>Still, it is becoming clear that the nation’s economic woes are not going to be fixed simply by continual rate-cutting. The attacks of Sept. 11 caught the Fed at just the wrong time Under the leadership of Alan Greenspan, it had slashed rates by three and a half percentage points between January and August m an attempt to juice up a sagging economy. The effects of rate cuts take a while to kick m, and the nation should have been starting to feel their influence right now. But the terrorist attacks took a big, one-time bite out of the economy that lower lending rates cannot fully address. Quick but careful action from Congress and the Bush administration is going to have to do the rest.</br></br>Cuts in the short-term federal lending rate can help businesses offer consumers easier credit, but they cannot make businesses invest in growth when sales are down, or make consumers suddenly worried about their jobs and portfolios decide to go shopping. Only intelligently targeted government spending — or, to a lesser extent, broad-based temporary tax cuts — can stimulate purchasing.</br></br>Cutting the federal funds rate also cannot lower long-term interest rates if the markets have no confidence in the stability of the federal budget. Worries that the Bush tax cut would aggravate future deficits are one reason that long-term rates stayed stubbornly high for much of this year, although they have fallen since the terrorist attack pushed a recovery further into the future.</br></br>Markets have been looking to the Fed’s announcements for soothing words of reassurance — the perception, if not the reality, of a guaranteed safety net. Had the Fed not cut rates again, markets would have slumped and faith in the Fed’s commitment to keep pumping up the economy would have dwindled. So the rate cut made some sense, but it will hardly be enough by itself

text: Stock market meltdowns have a lot of unpleasant consequences, fortunes lost, retirements ruined, college funds flattened, stock brokers unemployed. text: THERE is an American city where powerful people have swiftly responded to the nation's first recession in 10 years. About a week after Sept 11, they announced a new policy - call it a stimulus package -that has lifted the economy and probably prevented layoffs of thousands of additional workers</br></br>The city, of course, is not Washington, where officials in the White House and Capitol continue to proclaim a stimulus plan crucial but still cannot agree on what it should be</br></br>But 500 miles away, a group of prof it-driv-enexecutives have stepped into the void They work in Detroit, and they have provided a vivid example of just how effective</br></br>On Sept 19, General Motors announced that it would temporarily charge no interest on many loans, effectively cutting the price of a $25,000 car by more than $3,000. The move came on the same day that two members of President Bush's cabinet visited Detroit and urged industry officials to help the reeling economy Ford Motor and the domestic division of DaimlerChryslcr quickly took similar steps The deals remain in place for most models, and the results have exceeded nearly everyone’s expectations. Despite mounting layoffs and a pronounced shift toward conservative spending habits, consumers bought more vehicles in October than in any other month — ever. Across the economy, retail sales, which stopped growing during the summer and declined 2.4 percent in September, soared 7.1 percent in October, the government said last week The level or the response may have been surprising, but the reason for it was basic “The car companies put things on sale, and consumers are responding," said Richard J. DeKaser, the chief economist at the National City Corporation in Cleveland Knowing that the interest-free loans will not last forever, people have suddenly become willing to spend money that they would not otherwise This is economic stimulus.</br></br>Many of the proposals in Washington, by contrast, do almost nothing to alter people's calculations about whether they should spend money m the short term, economists say. And immediate spending is the key to preventing the economy from lapsing into a vicious cycle of lay-offs, weak consumer spending and yet more layoffs.

text: The number of workers filing new applications for jobless benefits increased by a seasonally adjusted 33,000, to 385,000, for the workweek ended Aug. 4, the Labor Department reported today. The four-week moving average has been down three weeks in a row.</br></br>In an effort to avert the first recession in the United States in II years, the Federal Reserve has cut short-term interest rates six times this year, totaling 2.75 percentage points. If the United States economy is not already in recession, it is on the brink of its first downturn in a decade. Why else would the Fed move with such urgency?</br></br>Obviously, a recession should be managed and contained. And if the Fed continues to cut interest rates over the next six months, as it should, it would help set the stage for the next upturn.</br></br>A mild recession, however, should not be feared. Recessions happen, and for a United States economy plagued with excesses, a downturn may be the only way to purge these reckless tendencies. The United</br></br>States has had five economic downturns since the 1970's, and these almost always purged the very excesses that can be most hazardous to economic health.</br></br>In the past, the excesses took the form of unwanted inventories, vacant office buildings, unneedcd factories or mounting inflation. The Federal Reserve usually stepped in when these imbalances got out of hand. Monetary tightening led to cuts in production, bringing inventories in better alignment with sales. Higher financing costs also tempered the zeal for overbuilding and for credit-based purchases of cars, furniture and appliances.

text: BUSINESS booms are famous for hiding underlying problems in an economy. It takes a recession to make them obvious.
